art-1.s: India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States, and the States and their territories are listed in the First Schedule. India's territory includes the States, the Union territories in the First Schedule, and any other territories India acquires.

art-2.s: Parliament can make a law to admit new States into the Union or to set up new States, on whatever terms and conditions it thinks fit.
k: how a new state is added

art-3.s: Parliament can by law create a new State, increase or reduce a State's area, change its boundaries or rename it. Such a Bill needs the President's recommendation, and if it affects a State, the President must first send it to that State's Legislature for its views within a set period.

art-4.s: A law admitting, creating or changing States under Article 2 or 3 must amend the First and Fourth Schedules as needed and may include related matters, such as representation in Parliament and State Legislatures. Such a law is not a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
k: new state law not constitutional amendment

art-5.s: A transitional rule for when the Constitution began: every person with domicile in India became a citizen if they were born in India, if either parent was born in India, or if they had ordinarily lived in India for at least five years just before.

art-6.s: A transitional rule: a person who migrated from what is now Pakistan counts as a citizen if they, a parent or a grandparent was born in India (as defined by the 1935 Act), and they either came before 19 July 1948 and have lived here since, or came later and registered after six months' residence.

art-7.s: A person who moved from India to what is now Pakistan after 1 March 1947 is not an Indian citizen, unless they came back under a permit for resettlement or permanent return. Such returnees are treated as having migrated to India after 19 July 1948.

art-8.s: A person living abroad who, or whose parent or grandparent, was born in India (as defined by the Government of India Act, 1935) counts as an Indian citizen if registered as one by India's diplomatic or consular representative in their country of residence.

art-9.s: A person who has voluntarily taken the citizenship of a foreign country is not an Indian citizen under Articles 5, 6 or 8.

art-10.s: Everyone who is, or is treated as, an Indian citizen under the earlier articles on citizenship continues to be a citizen, subject to any law Parliament makes.

art-11.s: Nothing in the earlier citizenship articles limits Parliament's power to make laws on gaining and ending citizenship and all other citizenship matters.

art-12.s: In the Fundamental Rights chapter, "the State" includes the Government and Parliament of India, each State's Government and Legislature, and all local or other authorities in India or under the Government of India's control.

art-13.s: Laws from before the Constitution that conflict with Fundamental Rights are void to that extent, and any law the State makes that takes away or reduces these rights is also void to that extent. "Law" includes ordinances, rules, regulations, notifications and customs with legal force, but constitutional amendments under Article 368 are not covered.

art-14.s: The State cannot deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws anywhere in India.

art-15.s: No citizen can face State discrimination, or be barred from shops, hotels, public wells and roads, only for religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. The State can make special provisions for women and children, backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and economically weaker sections, including in admissions, capping reservation for the last group at ten per cent.
k: special provisions for women and children

art-16.s: All citizens have equal opportunity in State jobs and offices, and no one can be denied them only for religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. Parliament can set residence rules, and the State can reserve posts for under-represented backward classes, promotions for Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and up to ten per cent for economically weaker sections.

art-17.s: Untouchability is abolished and practising it in any form is forbidden. Enforcing any disability arising from untouchability is an offence punishable by law.

art-18.s: The State cannot give titles other than military or academic distinctions, and Indian citizens cannot accept titles from foreign countries. Non-citizens holding an office of profit or trust under the State need the President's consent to accept foreign titles, and any such office holder needs it to accept foreign gifts, pay or offices.

art-19.s: Every citizen has the right to free speech and expression, to assemble peacefully without arms, to form associations, unions or co-operative societies, to move and settle anywhere in India, and to practise any profession or business. The State can place reasonable restrictions on these rights on stated grounds, such as public order, security, morality and the general public interest.

art-20.s: No one can be convicted except for breaking a law in force when the act was done, or given a heavier penalty than that law then allowed. No one can be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence, or forced to testify against themselves.

art-21.s: No person can be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

art-21A.s: The State must provide free and compulsory education to all children aged six to fourteen years, in the way it decides by law.

art-22.s: A person arrested must be told why, can consult their chosen lawyer, and must be brought before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time. This does not apply to enemy aliens or preventive detention, where holding someone over three months needs an Advisory Board report or a Parliament law, and the detainee must be told the grounds.

art-23.s: Trafficking in human beings, begar and other forced labour are banned, and breaking this rule is a punishable offence. The State can still require compulsory service for public purposes, but without discrimination only on religion, race, caste or class.

art-24.s: No child below fourteen years of age can be employed in a factory or mine or in any other hazardous work.

art-25.s: Everyone has an equal right to freedom of conscience and to freely profess, practise and spread religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights. The State can regulate secular activities linked to religion and make laws for social reform or to open public Hindu religious institutions to all Hindus; carrying kirpans is part of Sikh religion.

art-26.s: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or section of it has the right to set up and run religious and charitable institutions, manage its own religious affairs, and own, acquire and administer property according to law.

art-27.s: No one can be forced to pay taxes whose proceeds are specifically used to promote or maintain a particular religion or religious denomination.

art-28.s: Educational institutions wholly maintained by State funds cannot give religious instruction, unless the State runs one set up under an endowment or trust that requires it. In State-recognised or State-aided institutions, no one can be made to attend religious instruction or worship without their consent, or their guardian's consent if they are a minor.

art-29.s: Any group of citizens with its own distinct language, script or culture has the right to preserve it. No citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or State-aided educational institution only because of religion, race, caste or language.

art-30.s: All religious and linguistic minorities have the right to set up and run educational institutions of their choice. If the State acquires such an institution's property, the amount paid must not restrict this right, and the State cannot discriminate against minority-run institutions when giving aid.

art-31A.s: Laws letting the State acquire estates, temporarily manage property, merge corporations, or change rights of company managers, shareholders or mining leaseholders are not void for conflicting with Articles 14 or 19. State laws get this protection only with the President's assent, and land within a cultivator's ceiling limit can be acquired only at market value or more.

art-31B.s: Acts and Regulations listed in the Ninth Schedule are not void, and never were, for conflicting with Fundamental Rights, even if a court has ruled otherwise. They stay in force unless a competent legislature repeals or amends them.
k: laws protected from fundamental rights challenge

art-31C.s: A law carrying out the State's policy under Article 39(b) and (c), on sharing community resources for the common good and preventing concentration of wealth, is not void for conflicting with Articles 14 or 19, and State laws need the President's assent for this. The official notes say the Supreme Court struck down the 1976 widening to all Directive Principles, and the bar on courts checking whether a law really serves that policy.

art-32.s: Everyone has a guaranteed right to go to the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights, and the Court can issue directions, orders or writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. Parliament can give these powers to other courts, and this right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides.

art-33.s: Parliament can by law restrict or remove Fundamental Rights for members of the armed forces, forces keeping public order, intelligence or counter-intelligence bodies, and their telecommunication staff, to ensure they do their duties and keep discipline.

art-34.s: Parliament can by law protect government servants or others from liability for acts done to maintain or restore order in an area under martial law, and can validate sentences, punishments and other acts carried out under martial law there.

art-35.s: Only Parliament, not State Legislatures, can make laws on matters under Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and laws setting punishments for offences declared in the Fundamental Rights chapter, which Parliament must make soon after the Constitution began. Older laws on these matters stay in force until Parliament changes or repeals them.

art-36.s: In the Directive Principles chapter, "the State" has the same meaning as in the Fundamental Rights chapter.

art-37.s: Courts cannot enforce the Directive Principles, but they are fundamental to governing the country, and the State has a duty to apply them when making laws.
k: duty of state to apply directive principles

art-38.s: The State must strive for people's welfare through a social order where social, economic and political justice guides all national institutions. It must try to reduce income inequality and remove inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities among individuals and groups in different areas or occupations.

art-39.s: The State must aim its policy at adequate livelihood for men and women equally, sharing community resources for the common good, avoiding concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protecting workers and children from abuse, and healthy growth of children in freedom and dignity.

art-39A.s: The State must make sure the legal system promotes justice on equal terms and, in particular, provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities.

art-40.s: The State must take steps to organise village panchayats and give them the powers they need to work as units of self-government.

art-41.s: Within its economic capacity, the State must make effective provision for the right to work, to education, and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement and other undeserved need.

art-42.s: The State must provide for just and humane working conditions and for maternity relief.

art-43.s: The State must try to secure for all workers, agricultural, industrial or other, work, a living wage, decent working conditions, and full leisure and social and cultural opportunities. In particular, it must try to promote cottage industries in rural areas, run individually or as co-operatives.

art-43A.s: The State must take steps, through law or otherwise, to secure workers' participation in managing undertakings, establishments and other organisations in any industry.

art-43B.s: The State must try to promote co-operative societies that are voluntarily formed, run independently, democratically controlled and professionally managed.

art-44.s: The State must try to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.

art-45.s: The State must try to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age.

art-46.s: The State must, with special care, promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.

art-47.s: The State must treat raising nutrition levels, living standards and public health as among its primary duties, and in particular try to ban the consumption of intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs, except for medicinal purposes.

art-48.s: The State must try to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines, and in particular take steps to preserve and improve breeds and ban the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.

art-48A.s: The State must try to protect and improve the environment and safeguard the country's forests and wildlife.

art-49.s: The State must protect every monument, place or object of artistic or historic interest that a law of Parliament declares to be of national importance from damage, destruction, removal, disposal or export.

art-50.s: The State must take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in its public services.

art-51.s: The State must try to promote international peace and security, keep just and honourable relations between nations, encourage respect for international law and treaties, and encourage settling international disputes by arbitration.

art-51A.s: Every citizen has a duty to respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem, uphold India's unity, defend the country when called, promote harmony and women's dignity, protect heritage, the environment and public property, develop scientific temper, avoid violence, strive for excellence, and, as a parent or guardian, give children aged six to fourteen opportunities for education.

art-53.s: The Union's executive power belongs to the President, who uses it directly or through subordinate officers, and the President holds supreme command of the Defence Forces, as regulated by law. This does not move existing State functions to the President or stop Parliament from giving functions to other authorities.

art-54.s: The President is elected by an electoral college made up of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry.

art-55.s: Each elected State Assembly member's vote is worth the State's population divided by the Assembly's elected members, counted in thousands, and elected members of Parliament share the States' total votes equally. Voting uses proportional representation by single transferable vote and secret ballot, with population taken from the 1971 census until figures from the first census after 2026 are published.
k: value of vote in president election

art-56.s: The President holds office for five years from taking office and stays on until a successor takes over. The President can resign by writing to the Vice-President, who informs the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, or can be removed by impeachment for violating the Constitution.

art-57.s: A person who is or has been President can be elected again, subject to the other provisions of the Constitution.

art-58.s: To be elected President, a person must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha. They cannot hold an office of profit under any government or authority it controls, though being President, Vice-President, Governor or a Minister does not count.

art-59.s: The President cannot sit in Parliament or a State Legislature, so a member elected President loses that seat on taking office, and cannot hold any other office of profit. The President gets rent-free official residences and the pay, allowances and privileges Parliament sets, and pay and allowances cannot be cut during the term.

art-60.s: Before taking office, a President, or anyone acting as President, must swear or affirm before the Chief Justice of India, or the senior-most available Supreme Court Judge, to faithfully do the job, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and serve the people.

art-61.s: Either House of Parliament can charge the President with violating the Constitution, by a resolution moved on 14 days' written notice signed by one-fourth of its total members and passed by two-thirds of its total membership. The other House investigates, with the President able to appear, and its own two-thirds resolution upholding the charge removes the President.

art-62.s: A new President must be elected before the current term ends. If the office falls vacant through death, resignation, removal or otherwise, the election must be held as soon as possible and within six months, and the winner serves a full five-year term.

art-64.s: The Vice-President is automatically the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and cannot hold any other office of profit. While acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the Chairman's duties and does not get the Chairman's salary or allowances.
k: vice-president chairman of council of states

art-65.s: If the President's office falls vacant through death, resignation, removal or otherwise, the Vice-President acts as President until a newly elected President takes office. The Vice-President also carries out the President's functions during absence or illness, with the President's powers and immunities and pay set by Parliament or, until then, the Second Schedule.

art-66.s: Members of both Houses of Parliament elect the Vice-President by secret ballot, using proportional representation by single transferable vote. A candidate must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, qualified for the Rajya Sabha and not holding an office of profit under any government, and cannot remain a member of Parliament or a State Legislature.

art-67.s: The Vice-President serves five years and stays in office until a successor takes over. The Vice-President can resign in writing to the President, or be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all members of the Rajya Sabha and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, after at least 14 days' notice.

art-68.s: The election of a new Vice-President must be completed before the current term ends. If the office falls vacant through death, resignation, removal or otherwise, the election must be held as soon as possible, and the person elected serves a full five-year term.

art-69.s: Before taking office, the Vice-President must take an oath or affirmation before the President, or someone the President appoints, to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and faithfully carry out the duties of the office.

art-70.s: Parliament can make any arrangement it thinks fit for carrying out the President's functions in situations this Chapter does not cover.

art-71.s: The Supreme Court decides all doubts and disputes about the election of a President or Vice-President, and its decision is final. If an election is declared void, acts already done in office stay valid; Parliament can regulate these elections by law, and an election cannot be challenged just because of vacancies in the electoral college.

art-72.s: The President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions, or suspend, remit or commute sentences, in Court Martial cases, for offences against laws on matters within the Union's executive power, and in all death sentences. This does not affect Armed Forces officers' powers over Court Martial sentences or a Governor's legal powers over death sentences.

art-73.s: The Union's executive power covers matters on which Parliament can make laws and rights exercisable under treaties or agreements, but not, unless the Constitution or a law of Parliament says so, matters in a State on which the State Legislature can also make laws. Until Parliament provides otherwise, States can keep the executive powers they had before the Constitution began.

art-74.s: A Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister aids and advises the President, who must act on its advice. The President can ask it to reconsider, but must follow the advice given after reconsideration, and no court can inquire into what advice Ministers gave.
k: council of ministers advice to president
prime minister head of council of ministers

art-75.s: The President appoints the Prime Minister, and other Ministers on the Prime Minister's advice. Ministers, capped at 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha's total members, are collectively responsible to that House; a Minister not in either House for six consecutive months stops being one, and members disqualified under the Tenth Schedule cannot become Ministers for a period.
k: minister without being mp six months

art-76.s: The President appoints as Attorney-General for India a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. The Attorney-General advises the Government of India on legal matters, can be heard in all courts in India, and holds office at the President's pleasure with pay the President decides.

art-77.s: All executive action of the Government of India is taken in the President's name, and orders authenticated under the President's rules cannot be challenged as not made by the President. The President makes rules for conducting government business and dividing it among Ministers.
k: government orders in name of president
business rules of government of india

art-78.s: The Prime Minister must tell the President all Council of Ministers decisions on the Union's affairs and proposed laws, and give related information the President asks for. If the President requires, the Prime Minister must put before the Council any matter a Minister decided alone.
k: president right to information from pm

art-79.s: Parliament is made up of the President and two Houses: the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People).
k: council of states and house of the people

art-80.s: The Rajya Sabha has 12 members nominated by the President for special knowledge or experience in literature, science, art and social service, and up to 238 representatives of the States and Union territories. Elected members of each State's Legislative Assembly elect its representatives by single transferable vote, and Parliament decides how Union territory representatives are chosen.
k: how many members in council of states

art-81.s: The Lok Sabha has up to 530 members directly elected from State constituencies and up to 20 from Union territories. Seats are shared among States in proportion to population, with constituencies of similar population; until figures from the first census after 2026 are published, the 1971 census applies for State seats and the 2001 census for constituencies.
k: how many members in house of the people

art-82.s: After each census, State seats in the Lok Sabha and constituencies are readjusted as Parliament decides, from a date the President orders and not affecting the sitting House before its dissolution. Until figures from the first census after 2026 are published, seats based on the 1971 census and constituencies based on the 2001 census need not change.

art-83.s: The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved, and about one-third of its members retire every second year. The Lok Sabha lasts five years from its first meeting unless dissolved sooner; during an Emergency Parliament can extend this by law by up to one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the Emergency ends.
k: term of house of the people

art-84.s: To be chosen for Parliament, a person must be an Indian citizen, take an oath or affirmation before someone the Election Commission authorises, and meet qualifications Parliament sets. The minimum age is 30 for the Rajya Sabha, 25 for the Lok Sabha.
k: age to contest house of the people election

art-85.s: The President summons each House of Parliament when and where the President thinks fit, with less than six months between one session's last sitting and the next one's first. The President can also prorogue either or both Houses and dissolve the Lok Sabha.
k: dissolution of house of the people

art-86.s: The President can address either House of Parliament or both together and require members to attend. The President can also send messages to either House, about a pending Bill or anything else, and that House must consider the matter promptly.

art-87.s: At the start of the first session after each general election and of the first session each year, the President addresses both Houses together and tells Parliament why it has been summoned. Each House's rules must set aside time to discuss the address.
k: president address first session of year

art-88.s: Every Minister and the Attorney-General of India can speak and take part in either House, joint sittings and any parliamentary committee they are named to, but this right does not include voting.
k: can ministers speak in both houses
minister right to vote in other house

art-89.s: The Vice-President of India is automatically the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Council chooses one of its members as Deputy Chairman, and chooses another whenever that office falls vacant.

art-90.s: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha leaves office on ceasing to be a Council member, can resign in writing to the Chairman, and can be removed by a resolution of a majority of all Council members, after at least 14 days' notice.

art-91.s: When the Chairman's office is vacant or the Vice-President is acting as President, the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties, or, if that post is also vacant, a member the President appoints. When the Chairman is absent from a sitting, the Deputy Chairman presides, or else a person set by the Council's rules or chosen by the Council.

art-92.s: The Chairman cannot preside while a resolution to remove the Vice-President is being considered, nor the Deputy Chairman while one to remove the Deputy Chairman is. During the Vice-President's removal debate, the Chairman can speak and take part but cannot vote at all on that resolution or anything else in those proceedings.

art-93.s: The Lok Sabha chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker, and chooses a replacement whenever either office falls vacant.
k: deputy speaker house of the people

art-94.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker leaves office on ceasing to be a member of the Lok Sabha, can resign in writing to the other, and can be removed by a resolution of a majority of all the House's then members after 14 days' notice. On dissolution, the Speaker stays until just before the new House first meets.

art-95.s: When the Speaker's office is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs its duties, or else a member the President appoints. When the Speaker is absent from a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides, or else a person set by the House's rules or chosen by the House.

art-96.s: Neither the Speaker nor the Deputy Speaker can preside while a resolution to remove them is being considered. During a resolution to remove the Speaker, the Speaker can speak, take part and vote in the first instance, but cannot cast a tie-breaking vote.

art-97.s: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha get salaries and allowances fixed by Parliament by law, or those in the Second Schedule until then.
k: salary of chairman council of states

art-98.s: Each House of Parliament has its own secretarial staff, though posts common to both Houses can be created. Parliament can make laws on their recruitment and service conditions; until it does, the President makes rules after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be.

art-99.s: Before taking their seat, every member of either House of Parliament must take an oath or affirmation, in the form set out in the Third Schedule, before the President or a person the President appoints.

art-100.s: Questions in either House or a joint sitting are decided by a majority of members present and voting, and the presiding officer votes only to break a tie. A House can act despite vacancies, proceedings stay valid even if someone not entitled took part, and the quorum is one-tenth of total members, without which the meeting is adjourned or suspended.
k: majority of members present and voting

art-101.s: Nobody can sit in both Houses, or in Parliament and a State Legislature; a person chosen for both loses the Parliament seat unless they first resign the State seat. A seat falls vacant on disqualification or an accepted genuine resignation, and a House can declare vacant the seat of a member absent without permission for 60 days.

art-102.s: A person cannot be a member of Parliament if they hold an office of profit under the Union or a State government, unless Parliament exempts it, are declared of unsound mind by a court, are an undischarged insolvent, are not an Indian citizen or have taken foreign citizenship or allegiance, or are disqualified by Parliament's law or the Tenth Schedule.

art-103.s: If a question arises whether a member of Parliament has become disqualified under Article 102(1), the President decides it and the decision is final. Before deciding, the President must get the Election Commission's opinion and act according to it.

art-104.s: Anyone who sits or votes in either House before taking the required oath, or knowing they are not qualified, are disqualified or are barred by law, pays a penalty of 500 rupees for each such day, recovered as a debt owed to the Union.

art-105.s: There is freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and its rules. No member can face court proceedings for anything said or any vote in Parliament or its committees, nor anyone for publications under a House's authority; other privileges are whatever Parliament sets by law and, until it does, stay as they were before the 44th Amendment took effect in 1979. These protections also cover others entitled to speak in Parliament.

art-106.s: Members of Parliament receive salaries and allowances set by Parliament by law. Until then, they get the allowances that applied to members of the Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India just before the Constitution began.

art-107.s: Except for Money and other financial Bills, a Bill can start in either House and, apart from the joint sitting and Money Bill rules, passes only when both Houses agree to it and any amendments. Bills survive prorogation; on the Lok Sabha's dissolution, Bills pending in it, or passed by it and awaiting the Rajya Sabha, lapse, but others in the Rajya Sabha do not.
k: where can a bill be introduced

art-108.s: If one House rejects a Bill passed by the other, they finally disagree on amendments, or the other House does not pass it within six months, the President can summon a joint sitting, except for a Money Bill. The Bill passes if a majority of members of both Houses present and voting approve it, with only limited amendments allowed.

art-109.s: A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha. Once the Lok Sabha passes it, the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return it with recommendations, which the House can accept or reject; if not returned within 14 days, it counts as passed by both Houses as the Lok Sabha passed it.
k: money bill council of states 14 days
can council of states reject money bill

art-110.s: A Bill is a Money Bill only if it deals solely with matters like taxes, government borrowing or guarantees, the Consolidated or Contingency Fund of India, spending from or charged on the Consolidated Fund, public money receipts, audit, or related matters. Fines, fees or local taxes alone do not qualify, and the Speaker decides finally and certifies it.

art-111.s: When both Houses pass a Bill, the President gives or withholds assent. The President can return a Bill that is not a Money Bill for reconsideration, but if the Houses pass it again, with or without changes, the President cannot withhold assent.

art-112.s: Every financial year, the President has a statement of the Government of India's estimated receipts and spending laid before both Houses of Parliament. It shows separately spending charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, such as the President's pay, presiding officers' salaries, debt charges, Supreme Court judges' pay and court awards, and other spending from that Fund.

art-113.s: Spending charged on the Consolidated Fund of India can be discussed but not voted on in Parliament. Other spending goes to the Lok Sabha as demands for grants, which it can approve, refuse or reduce, and every demand needs the President's recommendation.

art-114.s: After the Lok Sabha votes the grants, a Bill is introduced to take from the Consolidated Fund of India the money for those grants and for charged expenditure. Neither House can amend it to change these amounts or purposes, and no money leaves the Fund without such a law.

art-115.s: If money approved for a service in a financial year proves too little, a new unplanned need arises, or more is spent than granted, the President places a fresh statement before both Houses or an excess demand before the Lok Sabha. The usual budget procedure then applies.

art-116.s: The Lok Sabha can grant money in advance for part of a year before the full budget is passed, grant money for an unexpected demand that cannot be detailed, and make an exceptional grant. Parliament can then authorise by law the withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India.

art-117.s: A Bill or amendment on money-bill matters needs the President's recommendation and cannot start in the Rajya Sabha, though amendments cutting or abolishing a tax need none, and fines, fees or local taxes alone do not make a Bill one. Bills involving spending from the Consolidated Fund of India also need the President's recommendation before either House passes them.

art-118.s: Each House of Parliament makes its own rules of procedure, using the old Dominion of India rules with changes until then. The President, after consulting the Chairman and the Speaker, makes rules for joint sittings and communication between the Houses, and the Speaker presides over joint sittings.

art-119.s: To finish financial business on time, Parliament can make a law on how each House handles financial matters and appropriation Bills. Where that law conflicts with a House's own rules, the law prevails.

art-120.s: Business in Parliament is done in Hindi or English, but the Chairman or Speaker can let a member who cannot express himself well in either speak in his mother-tongue. The text said "or in English" would drop out fifteen years after the Constitution began, in 1965, unless Parliament decided otherwise by law; Parliament's Official Languages Act, 1963 keeps English in use.

art-121.s: Parliament cannot discuss how a Supreme Court or High Court Judge behaved in doing their duties, except during a motion asking the President to remove that Judge.

art-122.s: Courts cannot question proceedings in Parliament on the ground of an irregular procedure. Members or officers who regulate procedure, business or order in Parliament are not subject to any court for using those powers.

art-123.s: Unless both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President can issue an Ordinance if satisfied that immediate action is needed. It has the force of an Act, but the President can withdraw it anytime, and it ends six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or earlier if both Houses disapprove.
k: how long does an ordinance last
law when parliament not in session

art-124.s: The Supreme Court has a Chief Justice and up to 37 other Judges (per the official note), appointed by the President. The text's National Judicial Appointments Commission route was struck down in 2015, so the earlier wording applies: appointment after consulting Supreme Court and High Court Judges. Judges serve until 65 and must be Indian citizens with five years as a High Court Judge, ten as a High Court advocate, or be a distinguished jurist in the President's view. A Judge can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by the President after each House votes for it by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.
k: how supreme court judges are appointed

art-124A.s: The Supreme Court struck down this article, with the rest of the 2014 amendment, on 16 October 2015, so the Commission does not operate. As written, it would have had the Chief Justice of India as chair, the next two senior Supreme Court Judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons chosen by the Prime Minister, Chief Justice and Opposition Leader, one of them from SC, ST, OBC, minority or women, each serving three years without renomination.

art-124B.s: Struck down by the Supreme Court on 16 October 2015 along with the 2014 amendment that created the National Judicial Appointments Commission, so it does not operate. As written, the Commission would have recommended people for appointment as Chief Justice of India, Supreme Court Judges, and High Court Chief Justices and Judges, recommended transfers of High Court Judges, and ensured those recommended had ability and integrity.

art-124C.s: Struck down by the Supreme Court on 16 October 2015 along with the 2014 amendment that created the National Judicial Appointments Commission, so it does not operate. As written, it let Parliament make a law on the procedure for appointing Supreme Court and High Court Judges and Chief Justices, and let the Commission set its own procedure and selection method by regulations.

art-125.s: Supreme Court Judges get salaries set by Parliament by law, or as listed in the Second Schedule until then. Parliament also decides their privileges, allowances, leave and pension, which cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

art-126.s: When the Chief Justice of India's office is vacant, or the Chief Justice cannot perform the duties, the President appoints another Supreme Court Judge to perform them.

art-127.s: If the Supreme Court lacks a quorum of Judges, the Chief Justice of India, with the President's prior consent and after consulting the High Court's Chief Justice, can ask a High Court Judge qualified for the Supreme Court to sit as a temporary (ad hoc) Judge. That Judge must give this priority and has full Supreme Court powers while attending. The text names the National Judicial Appointments Commission instead, but the Supreme Court struck down that 2014 change in 2015, so the earlier wording naming the Chief Justice applies.
k: high court judge in supreme court

art-128.s: With the President's consent, the Chief Justice of India can ask a former Supreme Court or Federal Court Judge, or a qualified former High Court Judge, to sit as a Supreme Court Judge. They sit only if willing, with a Judge's powers and allowances set by the President. The text names the National Judicial Appointments Commission, but the Supreme Court struck down that 2014 change in 2015, so the earlier wording naming the Chief Justice applies.

art-129.s: The Supreme Court is a court of record and has all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself.

art-130.s: The Supreme Court sits in Delhi, or in any other place the Chief Justice of India chooses with the President's approval.

art-131.s: Only the Supreme Court can hear disputes between the Government of India and States, or between States, that turn on a legal right. This excludes disputes from pre-Constitution treaties or agreements still in force, or ones that exclude this jurisdiction.

art-132.s: An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from any High Court judgment, decree or final order, civil, criminal or other, if the High Court certifies that it involves a substantial question on interpreting the Constitution. Any party can then appeal on the ground that the question was wrongly decided.

art-133.s: In civil cases, an appeal lies from a High Court to the Supreme Court if the High Court certifies a substantial question of law of general importance that the Supreme Court needs to decide, and a constitutional question can also be raised. Unless Parliament provides, no appeal lies from a single High Court Judge.
k: appeal from high court civil case

art-134.s: In criminal cases, an appeal lies from a High Court to the Supreme Court if the High Court reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death, took over a trial and gave a death sentence, or certifies the case as fit for appeal. Parliament can widen this by law.

art-134A.s: A High Court giving a judgment, decree, order or sentence covered by articles 132, 133 or 134 decides, on its own or when the aggrieved party asks orally right after, whether to grant a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court.
k: how to appeal to supreme court

art-135.s: Until Parliament decides otherwise, the Supreme Court also has any jurisdiction the Federal Court had under existing law before the Constitution began, for matters not covered by articles 133 or 134.

art-136.s: The Supreme Court can, at its discretion, give special leave to appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal in India, except those set up under laws on the Armed Forces.
k: appeal to supreme court from tribunal

art-137.s: The Supreme Court can review its own judgments or orders, subject to any law made by Parliament or rules made under article 145.

art-138.s: Parliament can by law give the Supreme Court more powers on Union List matters. The Government of India and a State can also give it more powers by special agreement, if Parliament provides by law.

art-139.s: Parliament can by law let the Supreme Court issue directions, orders or writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, for purposes other than enforcing fundamental rights under article 32.

art-139A.s: When the same important questions of law are pending in the Supreme Court and High Courts, or in several High Courts, the Supreme Court can take over and decide the cases, or decide the question and send them back. It can also move a case from one High Court to another for the ends of justice.
k: moving case to another high court

art-140.s: Parliament can by law give the Supreme Court extra powers, consistent with the Constitution, to help it use its jurisdiction more effectively.

art-141.s: Law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts in India.
k: are lower courts bound by supreme court

art-142.s: The Supreme Court can pass any decree or order needed for complete justice in a case before it, enforceable across India as Parliament or, until then, the President prescribes. Subject to Parliament's law, it can order people to attend, documents to be produced, and contempt to be investigated or punished.

art-143.s: If a question of law or fact of public importance arises or is likely to, the President can refer it to the Supreme Court, which can report its opinion after a hearing. The President can also refer disputes that article 131 leaves out.

art-144.s: All civil and judicial authorities in India must act in aid of the Supreme Court.

art-145.s: Subject to Parliament's law, the Supreme Court can make rules on its practice, with the President's approval, covering appeals, bail, fees, reviews and more. At least five Judges must hear cases on interpreting the Constitution and presidential references, and judgments are delivered in open Court with majority agreement, though Judges can dissent.

art-146.s: The Chief Justice of India, or a Judge or officer he directs, appoints Supreme Court staff and sets their service rules; the President may require UPSC consultation and must approve pay rules. The Court's administrative expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and its fees go into it.

art-147.s: In this Chapter and the High Courts chapter, a substantial question on interpreting the Constitution also includes questions on interpreting the Government of India Act, 1935, the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and orders made under them.

art-148.s: The President appoints the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, who can be removed only like a Supreme Court Judge and cannot hold further government office afterwards. Parliament sets the salary and service terms, which cannot be cut after appointment, and the office's expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

art-149.s: The Comptroller and Auditor-General performs duties and powers over the accounts of the Union, the States and other bodies as Parliament's law sets. Until then, the CAG has the powers the Auditor-General of India had before the Constitution began.

art-150.s: The President, on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, decides the form in which the accounts of the Union and the States are kept.

art-151.s: The Comptroller and Auditor-General's reports on Union accounts go to the President, who has them laid before each House of Parliament. Reports on a State's accounts go to the Governor, who has them laid before the State Legislature.

art-152.s: In this Part on the States, unless the context requires otherwise, "State" does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Jammu and Kashmir has been a Union territory, not a State, since 2019, so this exclusion no longer applies to any existing State.

art-153.s: Each State has a Governor. The same person can be appointed Governor of two or more States.

art-154.s: The State's executive power is vested in the Governor, who uses it directly or through subordinate officers under the Constitution. This does not move other authorities' existing legal functions to the Governor, or stop Parliament or the State Legislature giving functions to officers under the Governor.

art-155.s: The President appoints the Governor of a State by warrant under his hand and seal.

art-156.s: The Governor holds office at the President's pleasure and can resign in writing to the President. Otherwise the term is five years, and the Governor continues until a successor takes office.

art-157.s: To be appointed Governor, a person must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old.

art-158.s: The Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature, a member appointed Governor loses the seat, and the Governor cannot hold another office of profit. The Governor gets a rent-free residence and pay set by Parliament that cannot be reduced during the term, split among States by the President if shared.

art-159.s: Before taking office, every Governor, or person acting as Governor, takes an oath or affirmation before the State's High Court Chief Justice, or senior-most Judge available, to faithfully do the job, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and serve the State's people.

art-160.s: The President can make any arrangement he thinks fit for carrying out a Governor's functions in any situation this Chapter does not cover.

art-161.s: The Governor can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions, or suspend, remit or commute the sentence of anyone convicted under a law on a matter covered by the State's executive power.

art-162.s: A State's executive power covers matters on which its Legislature can make laws. On matters where both Parliament and the State can legislate, it is limited by executive power that the Constitution or Parliament's law gives the Union.

art-163.s: A Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor, except where the Governor must act in his discretion. The Governor's decision on what is discretionary is final, and courts cannot inquire into advice given by Ministers.

art-164.s: The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, and other Ministers on the Chief Minister's advice, all serving at the Governor's pleasure; there must be at least twelve Ministers and at most 15% of Assembly members. The Council is collectively responsible to the Assembly, and a Minister not in the Legislature for six consecutive months ceases to be one.

art-165.s: The Governor appoints as Advocate-General someone qualified to be a High Court Judge. The Advocate-General advises the State Government on legal matters and does assigned legal duties, holds office at the Governor's pleasure, and gets pay the Governor decides.

art-166.s: All executive action of a State Government is taken in the Governor's name, and orders authenticated under the Governor's rules cannot be challenged as not made by the Governor. The Governor makes rules for conducting government business and dividing it among Ministers.

art-167.s: The Chief Minister must tell the Governor all Council of Ministers decisions on running the State and proposed laws, give information the Governor asks for, and, if asked, put a single Minister's decision before the full Council.

art-168.s: Every State has a Legislature made up of the Governor and either one or two Houses. The text lists Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh as having two Houses, a Legislative Council and a Legislative Assembly, and adds Tamil Nadu under a law not yet in force. Other States have only a Legislative Assembly.

art-169.s: Parliament can make a law to abolish a State's Legislative Council, or create one where none exists, if the Legislative Assembly asks by a resolution passed by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting. Such a law can adjust the Constitution but does not count as an amendment under Article 368.

art-170.s: Each State Legislative Assembly has 60 to 500 members, directly elected from territorial constituencies with about equal population per seat. Seats and boundaries are readjusted after each census as Parliament decides by law, but until figures from the first census after 2026 are published, seat totals rest on the 1971 census and boundaries on the 2001 census.

art-171.s: A State's Legislative Council can have at most one-third as many members as its Legislative Assembly, and never fewer than 40. Unless Parliament decides otherwise, about one-third are elected by local bodies, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, one-third by Assembly members, and the rest are nominated by the Governor for knowledge of literature, science, art, co-operatives or social service.

art-172.s: A State Legislative Assembly lasts five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier. In an Emergency, Parliament can extend it by law one year at a time, up to six months after the Emergency ends. The Legislative Council is never dissolved; about one-third of its members retire every two years.

art-173.s: To be elected to a State Legislature, a person must be an Indian citizen, take an oath or affirmation before someone the Election Commission authorises, be at least 25 for the Assembly or 30 for the Council, and meet qualifications Parliament sets by law.

art-174.s: The Governor summons the State Legislature to meet, and no more than six months can pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. The Governor can also prorogue (end the session of) a House and dissolve the Assembly.

art-175.s: The Governor can address the Legislative Assembly, either House, or both Houses together, and require members to attend. The Governor can also send messages to the Houses, about a pending Bill or anything else, and the House must consider those matters promptly.

art-176.s: At the start of the first session after each general election and of the first session each year, the Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly, or both Houses together, and explains why it has been summoned. House rules must set aside time to discuss this address.

art-177.s: Every State Minister and the Advocate-General can speak and take part in the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly, the Legislative Council where one exists, and any legislative committee they are named to, but this right does not give them a vote.
k: can ministers speak in both houses

art-178.s: Each State Legislative Assembly chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as possible, and chooses another member whenever either post falls vacant.

art-179.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker loses the post on leaving the Assembly, can resign in writing to the other, and can be removed by a resolution of a majority of all the then members after at least 14 days' notice. If the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker stays on until just before the new Assembly first meets.

art-180.s: If the Speaker's post is vacant, the Deputy Speaker acts, or failing that, an Assembly member the Governor appoints. If the Speaker is absent from a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides, or else a person chosen under the Assembly's rules or by the Assembly.

art-181.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker cannot preside, even if present, while a resolution to remove them is under consideration. The Speaker can still speak and take part, and can vote in the first instance, but cannot cast a deciding vote in a tie.
k: can speaker vote on own removal

art-182.s: Each State Legislative Council chooses two of its members as Chairman and Deputy Chairman as soon as possible, and chooses another member whenever either post falls vacant.

art-183.s: The Chairman or Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council loses the post on leaving the Council, can resign in writing to the other, and can be removed by a resolution of a majority of all the then Council members after at least 14 days' notice.

art-184.s: If the Chairman's post is vacant, the Deputy Chairman acts, or failing that, a Council member the Governor appoints. If the Chairman is absent from a sitting, the Deputy Chairman presides, or else a person chosen under the Council's rules or by the Council.

art-185.s: The Chairman or Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council cannot preside, even if present, while a resolution to remove them is under consideration. The Chairman can still speak, take part and vote in the first instance, but not cast a deciding vote in a tie.
k: can chairman vote on own removal

art-186.s: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council are paid salaries and allowances fixed by State law, and until such a law is made, those set out in the Second Schedule.

art-187.s: Each House of a State Legislature has its own secretarial staff, though common posts for both Houses are allowed. State law can regulate their recruitment and service conditions; until then, the Governor makes rules after consulting the Speaker or Chairman.

art-188.s: Before taking their seat, every member of a State Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council must take an oath or affirmation, in the form set out in the Third Schedule, before the Governor or a person the Governor appoints.

art-189.s: Unless the Constitution says otherwise, a State Legislature decides by a majority of members present and voting, and the presiding officer votes only to break a tie. Vacancies or an unentitled participant do not invalidate proceedings. Unless State law provides otherwise, quorum is ten members or one-tenth of the House, whichever is greater; without it, the sitting must be adjourned or suspended.
k: majority of members present and voting

art-190.s: No one can sit in both Houses of a State Legislature, or in the Legislatures of two or more States. A seat becomes vacant on disqualification, or on a resignation the Speaker or Chairman accepts as voluntary and genuine. A House can declare a seat vacant if the member misses all its meetings for 60 days without permission.

art-191.s: A person is disqualified from a State Legislature for holding an office of profit under the Union or a State (Ministers and posts exempted by State law excepted), being declared of unsound mind by a court, being an undischarged insolvent, lacking Indian citizenship or owing allegiance to a foreign State, or disqualification by Parliament's law or the Tenth Schedule.

art-192.s: If a question arises whether a State legislator has become disqualified under Article 191(1), the Governor decides it and the decision is final. Before deciding, the Governor must get the Election Commission's opinion and act according to it.

art-193.s: Anyone who sits or votes in a State Legislature before taking the required oath, or knowing they are unqualified, disqualified or barred by law, must pay a penalty of five hundred rupees per day, recovered as a debt owed to the State.

art-194.s: State Legislatures have freedom of speech, subject to the Constitution and House rules. No member faces court proceedings for anything said or voted in the Legislature or its committees, nor anyone for the House's authorised publications. Other privileges are set by State law, or until then stay as before the Forty-fourth Amendment, and also cover non-members entitled to take part.

art-195.s: Members of a State's Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council receive salaries and allowances fixed by State law. Until such a law is made, they get what members of the corresponding Province's Legislative Assembly received just before the Constitution began.

art-196.s: In a two-House State, a Bill other than a Money or certain financial Bill can start in either House, and passes only when both agree to it, subject to the Assembly's power to override the Council under Articles 197 and 198. Prorogation does not make a pending Bill lapse. Dissolving the Assembly makes Bills pending in it, or passed by it and awaiting the Council, lapse, but not Bills pending only in the Council.
k: where can a bill be introduced

art-197.s: If the Legislative Council rejects a non-Money Bill passed by the Assembly, holds it over three months, or makes amendments the Assembly rejects, the Assembly can pass it again. If the Council then rejects it, holds it over one month, or again makes unacceptable amendments, the Bill counts as passed in the form the Assembly passed it the second time.

art-198.s: A Money Bill cannot start in the Legislative Council. After the Assembly passes it, the Council has 14 days to return it with recommendations, which the Assembly can accept or reject. It then counts as passed by both Houses with only the accepted changes, or as the Assembly passed it if not returned in time.

art-199.s: A Money Bill deals only with taxes, State borrowing or guarantees, the Consolidated or Contingency Fund, spending from or charged on the Consolidated Fund, receipts into State accounts, or related matters. Fines, licence or service fees, or local taxes alone do not make it one. The Assembly Speaker decides finally and certifies it.
k: money bill vs fees and fines

art-200.s: A Bill passed by the State Legislature goes to the Governor, who can assent, withhold assent, or reserve it for the President. The Governor can return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration, but must assent if it is passed again. A Bill that would cut the High Court's powers enough to endanger its constitutional role must be reserved for the President.

art-201.s: When a Governor reserves a Bill for the President, the President assents or withholds assent. For a non-Money Bill, the President can have it returned to the Legislature, which must reconsider it within six months; if passed again, it goes back to the President.

art-202.s: Each financial year, the Governor has the State's estimated receipts and spending, called the annual financial statement, laid before the Legislature. It separates spending charged on the Consolidated Fund from other spending, and revenue spending from the rest. Charged spending includes the Governor's pay, presiding officers' salaries, State debt charges, High Court judges' salaries and court or tribunal awards.

art-203.s: Spending charged on the State's Consolidated Fund can be discussed but not voted on by the Assembly. Other spending comes as demands for grants, which the Assembly can approve, reject or reduce. Every demand for a grant needs the Governor's recommendation.

art-204.s: After the Assembly votes grants, a Bill authorises drawing money from the State's Consolidated Fund for those grants and for charged spending, within the amounts laid before the House. No amendment may change these amounts or purposes; the presiding officer decides finally. Apart from Articles 205 and 206, money leaves the Fund only under such a law.

art-205.s: If approved money for a service proves insufficient, a new unplanned service needs funds, or more was spent than granted, the Governor must lay a further statement before the Legislature or present a demand for the excess to the Assembly. The usual budget procedures in Articles 202 to 204 apply to these.

art-206.s: Apart from the normal budget process, the Legislative Assembly can grant money in advance for part of a year until the budget is passed, grant money for an unexpected need too large or vague to detail, or make an exceptional grant outside the year's normal services. The Legislature can authorise withdrawals for these by law, following Articles 203 and 204.

art-207.s: Bills or amendments on the money matters listed in Article 199 need the Governor's recommendation and cannot start in the Legislative Council, except amendments to cut or abolish a tax. Fines, fees or local taxes alone do not count. A Bill involving spending from the State's Consolidated Fund cannot be passed unless the Governor recommends its consideration.

art-208.s: Each House of a State Legislature makes its own rules of procedure and business, subject to the Constitution. Until it does, the corresponding Province's rules from just before the Constitution began apply, as adapted by the Speaker or Chairman. In a two-House State, the Governor makes rules on communication between the Houses after consulting both presiding officers.

art-209.s: To finish financial business on time, a State Legislature can make a law regulating how its Houses handle financial matters and appropriation Bills. Where such a law conflicts with the Houses' own rules or standing orders, the law prevails.

art-210.s: State Legislatures do business in the State's official language or languages, Hindi or English, and the presiding officer can let a member who cannot express themselves in these use their mother tongue. Unless State law says otherwise, the English option ends fifteen years after the Constitution began (twenty-five for Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura; forty for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram).
k: speak in mother tongue in assembly

art-211.s: A State Legislature cannot discuss how any Supreme Court or High Court Judge has conducted themselves in carrying out their duties.

art-212.s: The validity of proceedings in a State Legislature cannot be questioned on the ground of irregular procedure. Officers or members empowered to regulate procedure, conduct business or keep order in the Legislature are not subject to any court's jurisdiction over how they use those powers.

art-213.s: When the State Legislature is not in session and immediate action is needed, the Governor can issue Ordinances, though some need the President's instructions. An Ordinance works like a State law but lapses six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, or sooner if disapproved. The Governor can withdraw it, and it is void where a State law would be invalid.

art-214.s: Every State has a High Court.

art-215.s: Every High Court is a court of record, with all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself.

art-216.s: Every High Court has a Chief Justice and as many other Judges as the President decides from time to time are needed.

art-217.s: The President appoints High Court Judges by warrant after consulting the Chief Justice of India, the State's Governor and, for Judges other than the Chief Justice, the High Court's Chief Justice. The text's reference to the National Judicial Appointments Commission comes from a 2014 amendment the Supreme Court struck down on 16 October 2015. Judges serve until 62 unless they resign in writing or are removed like a Supreme Court Judge, and must be Indian citizens with at least ten years in judicial office or as a High Court advocate.

art-218.s: The process for removing Judges set out in clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 for the Supreme Court also applies to High Court Judges, with references to the Supreme Court read as the High Court.

art-219.s: Before taking office, every new High Court Judge must take an oath or affirmation before the State's Governor, or a person the Governor appoints, in the form given in the Third Schedule.

art-220.s: A person who has served as a permanent High Court Judge since the Constitution began cannot later argue cases or act in any court or before any authority in India, except the Supreme Court and other High Courts.
k: can retired high court judge practise

art-221.s: Parliament sets the salaries, allowances, leave and pension of High Court Judges by law, and until it does, the Second Schedule applies. A Judge's allowances, leave or pension cannot be changed to the Judge's disadvantage after appointment.

art-222.s: The President can transfer a Judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India. The text's reference to a National Judicial Appointments Commission recommendation comes from a 2014 amendment the Supreme Court struck down on 16 October 2015. A transferred Judge gets a compensatory allowance on top of salary, fixed by Parliament by law or, until then, by the President.

art-223.s: When the post of a High Court Chief Justice is vacant, or the Chief Justice cannot perform the duties due to absence or another reason, the President appoints one of the other Judges of that Court to perform them.

art-224.s: If a High Court's work temporarily increases or piles up, the President can appoint qualified additional Judges for up to two years, and can appoint an acting Judge while a Judge is absent or acting as Chief Justice; neither may serve past age 62. The text's requirement to consult the National Judicial Appointments Commission comes from a 2014 amendment the Supreme Court struck down on 16 October 2015.

art-224A.s: The Chief Justice of a High Court, with the President's prior consent, can ask a former Judge of that or any other High Court to sit as a Judge there. The person must agree, gets allowances fixed by the President, and has a Judge's powers while sitting. The text's version giving this role to the National Judicial Appointments Commission comes from a 2014 amendment the Supreme Court struck down on 16 October 2015.

art-225.s: Existing High Courts keep the same jurisdiction, law, and Judges' powers, including making court rules and arranging sittings, as just before the Constitution began, subject to the Constitution and laws of the appropriate Legislature. Old limits on their original jurisdiction in revenue matters no longer apply.

art-226.s: Every High Court can issue orders or writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, to any person, authority or government in its area, to enforce Part III rights or for any other purpose. An interim order made without hearing a party lapses if the Court does not decide that party's plea to cancel it within two weeks.

art-227.s: Every High Court supervises all courts and tribunals in its territory, except those set up under armed forces law. It can call for returns, make rules and forms for their practice and record-keeping, and set fees for their staff and lawyers, but these must follow existing law and need the Governor's prior approval.

art-228.s: If a case in a lower court raises a substantial question of law about interpreting the Constitution that must be answered to decide it, the High Court takes over the case. It can then decide the whole case, or answer the question and send the case back to be decided accordingly.

art-229.s: The Chief Justice of a High Court, or a Judge or officer the Chief Justice directs, appoints the Court's staff and makes rules on their service, subject to State law, with pay, leave and pension rules needing the Governor's approval. The Court's administrative expenses are charged on the State's Consolidated Fund, and its fees go into that Fund.

art-230.s: Parliament can by law extend a High Court's jurisdiction to a Union territory or remove it. Where a State's High Court covers a Union territory, the State Legislature cannot change that jurisdiction, and the President, not the Governor, approves rules for that territory's lower courts.

art-231.s: Parliament can by law set up a common High Court for two or more States, or for two or more States and a Union territory. The Governors of all the States it serves take the Governor's part in appointing its Judges (a 2014 amendment removed this rule, but it was struck down in 2015). Its oath, staff and expense rules follow the State of its principal seat, or the Union if that seat is in a Union territory, and each State's Governor approves rules for that State's lower courts.
k: one high court for two states

art-232.s: No current text. Articles 230, 231 and 232 were replaced in 1956 by the present Articles 230 and 231, so this number is now empty.

art-233.s: The Governor appoints, posts and promotes district judges in consultation with the High Court. Someone not already serving the Union or the State can become a district judge only after at least seven years as an advocate or pleader and on the High Court's recommendation.

art-233A.s: A validation rule: district judge appointments, postings, promotions and transfers made before the Twentieth Amendment of 1966 without following Articles 233 or 235 are not invalid for that reason alone, and neither are those judges' judgments, orders and other acts, despite any court ruling.

art-234.s: The Governor appoints people other than district judges to a State's judicial service, under rules the Governor makes after consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.

art-235.s: The High Court controls district courts and the courts below them, including posting, promoting and granting leave to judicial officers below district judge. These officers keep any right of appeal under their service law, and the High Court must deal with them according to their service conditions.

art-236.s: In this Chapter, a 'district judge' includes city civil court judges, additional, joint and assistant district judges, chief small cause court judges, chief and additional chief presidency magistrates, and sessions, additional and assistant sessions judges. 'Judicial service' means a service only of people meant to fill district judge and lower civil judicial posts.

art-237.s: The Governor can, by public notification, apply this Chapter's provisions and rules on the judicial service to any class of magistrates in the State, from a date the Governor fixes and with any exceptions or changes stated in the notification.

art-239.s: Unless Parliament provides otherwise by law, the President runs every Union territory, acting as far as the President thinks fit through an administrator the President appoints. The President can make a neighbouring State's Governor the administrator, who then acts independently of the State's Council of Ministers.

art-239A.s: Parliament can by law create for Puducherry an elected or partly nominated Legislature, a Council of Ministers, or both, with the powers it specifies. Such a law does not count as a constitutional amendment under Article 368, even if it changes the Constitution.

art-239AA.s: Delhi is the National Capital Territory, with an elected Legislative Assembly that can legislate on State and Concurrent List matters except State List Entries 1, 2 and 18 (public order, police and land). Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes, and one-third will be reserved for women once the post-census delimitation under Article 334A happens. A Chief Minister-led Council of Ministers advises the Lieutenant Governor, who refers disagreements to the President, and Parliament's laws generally prevail over conflicting Assembly laws.

art-239AB.s: If the President, on the Lieutenant Governor's report or otherwise, is satisfied that Delhi cannot be run under Article 239AA, or that it is needed for proper administration, the President can suspend any part of Article 239AA or laws made under it and make arrangements to run Delhi.

art-239B.s: When Puducherry's Legislature is not in session, its administrator can issue Ordinances for urgent action, but only on the President's instructions and never while the Legislature is dissolved or suspended. An Ordinance works like a law of the Legislature but lapses six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, or earlier if the Legislature disapproves it.

art-240.s: The President can make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Puducherry, and these can amend or repeal Acts of Parliament applying there. For Puducherry, this power stops once its Legislature first meets, except while it is dissolved or suspended.

art-241.s: Parliament can by law create a High Court for a Union territory or declare a court there to be a High Court, and the rules for State High Courts apply with any changes Parliament makes. High Courts already covering a Union territory before 1956 continue to do so.

art-243.s: Key terms for the Panchayat Part: a Panchayat is a rural self-government body, the Gram Sabha is the people on the village electoral rolls, the Governor notifies what counts as a village and the intermediate level, and population means the last published census figures.

art-243A.s: A Gram Sabha can exercise the powers and perform the functions at village level that the State Legislature gives it by law.

art-243B.s: Every State must have Panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels, but a State with a population of up to twenty lakh need not set up the intermediate level.

art-243C.s: The State Legislature decides how Panchayats are composed, keeping population per seat roughly equal, and all seats are filled by direct election. It can add lower-level Chairpersons and MPs and State legislators from the area as members, all members can vote, and higher-level Chairpersons are elected by and from the elected members.

art-243D.s: Every Panchayat reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their local population, and at least one-third of all directly elected seats, counting SC and ST women, for women, with seats rotated. Chairperson posts are also reserved for SCs, STs and women (at least one-third), and States may add reservations for backward classes.

art-243E.s: A Panchayat lasts five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier, and changing a law cannot cut short its term. Elections must be held before the term ends, or within six months of a dissolution unless less than six months would remain, and a replacement Panchayat serves only the remaining term.

art-243F.s: A person is disqualified from being a Panchayat member if disqualified under any law for State Legislature elections or under a State law, but no one aged 21 or more is barred for being under 25. A State law decides who rules on disqualification disputes.

art-243G.s: The State Legislature can by law give Panchayats the powers they need to work as institutions of self-government, including preparing and carrying out plans and schemes for economic development and social justice, such as on matters in the Eleventh Schedule.

art-243H.s: The State Legislature can by law let Panchayats levy, collect and keep taxes, duties, tolls and fees, assign them taxes collected by the State, give them grants from the State's Consolidated Fund, and set up funds for their money.

art-243-I.s: The Governor sets up a Finance Commission every five years to review Panchayat finances and recommend how State taxes are shared or assigned, what grants they get, and how to improve their finances. The State Legislature decides its membership and powers, and its recommendations and the action taken go before the Legislature.

art-243J.s: The State Legislature can make laws on how Panchayats keep accounts and how those accounts are audited.

art-243K.s: A State Election Commission, made up of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor, controls electoral rolls and all Panchayat elections. The Commissioner can be removed only like a High Court Judge, their service terms cannot be worsened after appointment, and the Governor provides staff on request.

art-243L.s: The Panchayat provisions also apply to Union territories, with the Administrator in place of the Governor and any Legislative Assembly in place of the State Legislature. The President can, by public notification, apply them with exceptions or changes.

art-243M.s: Panchayat rules do not apply to Scheduled and tribal areas under Article 244, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Manipur hill areas with District Councils, or (at district level) Darjeeling's hill areas, and Scheduled Caste seat reservation skips Arunachal Pradesh. Those three States, by special Assembly majority, or Parliament for Scheduled and tribal areas, can extend this Part by law.
k: where panchayat rules do not apply

art-243N.s: A transitional rule from 1992: State Panchayat laws that conflict with this Part stayed in force until changed, but for no more than one year. Existing Panchayats could finish their terms unless the State Legislature dissolved them earlier.

art-243P.s: Defines key terms for the Municipalities Part, such as a Metropolitan area: an area of ten lakhs or more people, covering one or more districts and two or more Municipalities or Panchayats, notified by the Governor. Population means the count at the last published census.

art-243Q.s: Every State must set up a Nagar Panchayat for an area changing from rural to urban, a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area, and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. The Governor classifies areas by population, density, revenue, non-agricultural jobs and similar factors, and can exempt industrial townships.

art-243R.s: Municipality seats are filled by direct election from wards. The State Legislature can also, by law, add experts in municipal administration (who cannot vote), Lok Sabha and Assembly members whose constituencies cover the area, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council members registered there, and chairpersons of the other committees set up under Article 243S(5), and decide how the Chairperson is elected.

art-243S.s: Every Municipality with a population of three lakhs or more must have Wards Committees of one or more wards, which include the Municipality's members for those wards.
