The ward member chairs it or, for several wards, one of those ward members elected by the Committee does, and States decide the rest and can create other committees.

art-243T.s: Municipality seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their local population, with at least one-third of those for SC or ST women, and at least one-third of all directly elected seats go to women. States decide Chairperson reservations and can reserve for backward classes, and SC and ST reservations end after the Article 334 period.

art-243U.s: A Municipality serves five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier after a reasonable hearing, and a change in law cannot cut a sitting Municipality's term short. Elections must finish before the term ends or within six months of dissolution, unless under six months remain, and a replacement body serves only the remaining term.

art-243V.s: A person cannot be or become a Municipality member if disqualified under laws for State Legislature elections or any State law, though nobody aged 21 or more is disqualified for being under 25. The State Legislature sets who decides disqualification questions.

art-243W.s: The State Legislature can, by law, give Municipalities the powers they need as institutions of self-government, including preparing plans for economic development and social justice and carrying out schemes on Twelfth Schedule matters. It can also empower committees to do their duties.

art-243X.s: The State Legislature can, by law, let Municipalities levy and collect taxes, duties, tolls and fees, hand them taxes collected by the State, give them grants from the State's Consolidated Fund, and set up funds to hold and pay out their money.

art-243Y.s: The State Finance Commission under Article 243I also reviews Municipalities' finances and recommends to the Governor how State taxes and fees are shared with them, which taxes they get, what grants they receive and how to improve their finances. The Governor places its recommendations and an action-taken note before the State Legislature.

art-243Z.s: The State Legislature can make laws on how Municipalities keep their accounts and how those accounts are audited.

art-243ZA.s: The State Election Commission oversees and controls the preparation of voter lists and the conduct of all Municipality elections. The State Legislature can make laws on any matter relating to these elections.

art-243ZB.s: The Municipalities Part applies to Union territories, with the Administrator replacing the Governor and any Union territory Legislative Assembly replacing the State Legislature. The President can, by public notification, apply it to any Union territory with exceptions and changes.

art-243ZC.s: The Municipalities Part does not apply to Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under Article 244, and it does not affect the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's powers. Parliament can extend it to those areas by law, with exceptions, and such a law does not count as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
k: where municipality rules do not apply

art-243ZD.s: Every State must set up District Planning Committees to combine Panchayat and Municipality plans into a draft development plan for each district, considering shared resources, and send it to the State Government. At least four-fifths of members are elected by and from elected local body members, in proportion to rural and urban population.

art-243ZE.s: Every Metropolitan area must have a Metropolitan Planning Committee to prepare a draft development plan for the whole area, considering local plans, shared resources, government priorities and investment, and send it to the State Government. At least two-thirds of members are elected by and from elected Municipality members and Panchayat chairpersons, in proportion to their populations.

art-243ZF.s: A transitional rule from 1992: State Municipality laws that conflict with this Part stayed in force for at most one year after the Seventy-fourth Amendment unless changed sooner. Existing Municipalities could finish their terms unless dissolved earlier by a resolution of the State Legislature.

art-243ZG.s: Courts cannot question laws on drawing Municipality constituencies or allotting seats to them. A Municipality election can be challenged only through an election petition, before the authority and in the way set by State law.

art-243ZH.s: Defines key terms for the co-operative societies Part. A board is the body that manages a society's affairs, a multi-State co-operative society has objects beyond one State, office bearers include the President, Chairperson, Secretary and Treasurer, and the Registrar is appointed by the Central or State Government.

art-243Z-I.s: The State Legislature can make laws on forming, regulating and winding up co-operative societies, based on voluntary formation, democratic member control, member economic participation and autonomous functioning.

art-243ZJ.s: A co-operative board can have at most 21 directors, with one seat for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes and two for women where such members exist, and elected members and office bearers serve five years. States must allow up to two co-opted experts, who cannot vote in society elections or become office bearers.

art-243ZK.s: A co-operative board's election must be held before its term ends, so new members take office as soon as the old board's term expires. An authority set up by State law oversees voter lists and the conduct of all co-operative society elections.

art-243ZL.s: A co-operative board can be superseded or suspended for at most six months (one year for a co-operative bank that is not multi-State), only for reasons like persistent default, negligence, harmful acts, deadlock or failed elections, and only where the Government has a shareholding, loan, aid or guarantee. The administrator must hold elections and hand over.

art-243ZM.s: The State Legislature can make laws on co-operative society accounts and an audit at least once each financial year, and must set minimum qualifications for auditors. The society's general body appoints auditors from a State-approved panel, the audit must finish within six months of the financial year's end, and apex societies' audit reports go before the State Legislature.

art-243ZN.s: The State Legislature can require every co-operative society to hold its annual general body meeting within six months of the end of the financial year.

art-243ZP.s: Every co-operative society must file returns within six months of each financial year's end with the authority named by the State Government, including its annual report, audited accounts, plan for using surplus, bye-law changes, dates of meetings and elections, and any information the Registrar requires.

art-243ZQ.s: The State Legislature can make laws on co-operative society offences and penalties. These must include wilfully giving false returns or information, disobeying summons or lawful written orders, employers not paying over deducted amounts within fourteen days, failing to hand over society records or property, and corrupt practices in board elections.

art-243ZR.s: The co-operative societies Part also applies to multi-State co-operative societies, with Parliament, Central Acts and the Central Government taking the place of the State Legislature, State Acts and the State Government.

art-243ZS.s: The co-operative societies Part applies to Union territories, with the Administrator replacing the State Legislature where there is no Legislative Assembly, and the Assembly where there is one. The President can, by notification in the Official Gazette, exclude any Union territory or part of one.

art-243ZT.s: A transitional rule from 2011: State co-operative laws that conflict with this Part stayed in force for at most one year after the Ninety-seventh Amendment, unless amended or repealed sooner.

art-244.s: The Fifth Schedule governs the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Sixth Schedule governs the administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

art-244A.s: Parliament can, by law, create an autonomous State within Assam from Sixth Schedule tribal areas, with its own Legislature, Council of Ministers, or both, and set its law-making and executive powers and share of Assam's taxes. Changing those powers needs two-thirds of members present and voting in each House, and such a law is not a constitutional amendment.

art-245.s: Parliament can make laws for all or part of India, and a State Legislature can make laws for all or part of its State. A law made by Parliament is not invalid just because it operates outside India's territory.

art-246.s: Only Parliament can make laws on Union List subjects and only a State Legislature on State List subjects for its State, while both can legislate on Concurrent List subjects, all set out in the Seventh Schedule. Parliament can also legislate on State List subjects for any part of India not in a State.
k: union list state list concurrent list
who can make laws on what subject

art-246A.s: Parliament and every State Legislature can make laws on goods and services tax imposed by the Union or that State. Only Parliament can make GST laws where goods or services are supplied in inter-State trade or commerce.

art-247.s: Parliament can, by law, set up additional courts to better administer laws made by Parliament or existing laws on Union List subjects.

art-248.s: Only Parliament can make laws on any subject not listed in the Concurrent List or State List, including taxes not mentioned in either list, subject to the special rule on goods and services tax.

art-249.s: If the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is in the national interest, Parliament can make laws on a State List subject or GST. The resolution lasts up to one year and can be renewed a year at a time, and such laws lapse six months after it ends.

art-250.s: While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament can make laws for all or part of India on any State List subject or GST. Such laws stop having effect six months after the Emergency ends, except for things already done.

art-251.s: A State keeps its own law-making power despite Articles 249 and 250, but if a State law conflicts with a Parliament law made under them, the Parliament law prevails. The State law does not operate to that extent while the Parliament law is in effect.
k: conflict between central and state law

art-252.s: If the Legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions asking Parliament to make a law on a matter it normally cannot legislate on for States, Parliament can do so for them, and other States can adopt it by resolution. Only Parliament, acting the same way, can amend or repeal it, not the States.
k: states ask parliament to make law
law for two or more states

art-253.s: Parliament can make laws for all or part of India to implement any treaty, agreement or convention with other countries, or any decision taken at an international conference, association or other body.

art-254.s: If a State law conflicts with a Parliament law, or with an existing law on a Concurrent List subject, the Parliament or existing law prevails and the State law is void to that extent. A conflicting State law on a Concurrent subject prevails in that State with the President's assent, but Parliament can still change it.

art-255.s: An Act of Parliament or a State Legislature is not invalid only because a recommendation or prior sanction was missing, if assent came from the Governor or President (for a Governor's recommendation), the Rajpramukh or President (for a Rajpramukh's), or the President (for his own).

art-256.s: Every State must use its executive power to ensure that laws made by Parliament and existing laws applying in that State are followed, and the Union can give a State any directions the Government of India finds necessary for this.

art-257.s: States must use their executive power without obstructing the Union's, and the Government of India can direct them to ensure this. It can also direct States to build and maintain communications of national or military importance and to protect railways, paying extra costs as agreed or as fixed by an arbitrator the Chief Justice of India appoints.
k: roads of national or military importance

art-258.s: With a State government's consent, the President can hand over Union functions to that government or its officers, with or without conditions. A law of Parliament can also give powers and duties to a State, and the Government of India pays the extra administrative costs, as agreed or as fixed by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.

art-258A.s: With the consent of the Government of India, a State's Governor can hand over State functions to the Government of India or its officers, with or without conditions.
k: governor hand over powers to union

art-260.s: The Government of India can, by agreement with the government of a territory outside India, take on that territory's executive, legislative or judicial functions. Such agreements must follow the law on foreign jurisdiction in force at the time.

art-261.s: Public acts, records and court proceedings of the Union and every State get full faith and credit across India, with their proof and effect set by Parliament by law. Final civil court judgments or orders can be enforced anywhere in India according to law.
k: enforce civil court judgment in another state

art-262.s: Parliament can make laws to settle disputes or complaints about the use, distribution or control of the waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys. It can also bar the Supreme Court and all other courts from hearing such disputes.

art-263.s: If the President thinks it serves the public interest, the President can by order set up a Council to advise on disputes between States, study subjects of common interest, and recommend better policy coordination. The order sets its duties, organisation and procedure.

art-264.s: In this Part, "Finance Commission" means the Finance Commission set up under article 280.

art-265.s: No tax can be levied or collected unless a law authorises it.
k: can government tax without a law

art-266.s: All revenues, loans raised and loan repayments received by the Government of India form the Consolidated Fund of India, and those of each State form the Consolidated Fund of the State. Other public money goes into the public account of India or of the State. Money leaves a Consolidated Fund only according to law and the Constitution.

art-267.s: Parliament can by law create a Contingency Fund of India, placed at the President's disposal, to make advances for unforeseen spending until Parliament approves that spending by law. A State Legislature can create a similar Contingency Fund of the State, placed at the Governor's disposal.

art-268.s: Stamp duties in the Union List are imposed by the Government of India but collected by the States where they apply, or by the Union in Union territories. Proceeds collected in a State go to that State, not the Consolidated Fund of India.

art-269.s: The Government of India levies and collects taxes on inter-State sale or purchase of goods (other than newspapers) and on inter-State consignment of goods, except as article 269A provides. The net proceeds, except from Union territories, go to the States concerned, shared on principles set by Parliament, which can also define when a transaction is inter-State.
k: tax on inter-state sale of goods

art-269A.s: The Government of India levies and collects goods and services tax (GST) on inter-State supplies, including imports, and Parliament by law, on the GST Council's recommendations, splits it between the Union and the States. A State's share stays out of the Consolidated Fund of India. Parliament can define place of supply and when a supply is inter-State.
k: gst sharing between centre and states

art-270.s: Union List taxes and duties, except those under articles 268, 269 and 269A, surcharges and special-purpose cesses, are collected by the Government of India and shared with the States, as are certain GST amounts. The States' share of net proceeds, and its division among them, is set by Presidential order after considering Finance Commission recommendations.
k: sharing of taxes between centre and states

art-271.s: Parliament can at any time add a surcharge for Union purposes to the duties and taxes in articles 269 and 270, except GST under article 246A. The whole surcharge goes into the Consolidated Fund of India.
k: union surcharge not shared with states

art-273.s: A transitional rule: instead of a share of jute export duty, Assam, Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal got yearly grants from the Consolidated Fund of India while the duty continued or for ten years from the Constitution's start, whichever was earlier. The grants therefore ended by 1960 at the latest.
k: grants to assam bihar odisha west bengal

art-274.s: Without the President's recommendation, no Bill or amendment can be introduced in Parliament that imposes or changes a tax or duty in which States are interested, changes the meaning of "agricultural income" for income-tax, affects how money is shared with States, or imposes a Union surcharge. Such taxes are those whose proceeds go to, or decide payments to, States.

art-275.s: Parliament can provide yearly grants from the Consolidated Fund of India to States needing help. States also get grants for approved schemes for Scheduled Tribes' welfare and Scheduled Areas' administration, with special grants for Assam's tribal areas and any autonomous State under article 244A. Until Parliament acts, the President decides, considering Finance Commission recommendations.

art-276.s: A State law taxing professions, trades, callings or employments, for the State or a local body, is not invalid just because it is a tax on income. The total one person pays to the State or to any one local body cannot exceed two thousand five hundred rupees a year. Parliament's power to tax income from these activities is unaffected.

art-277.s: Taxes, duties, cesses or fees lawfully levied by a State or local body just before the Constitution began can continue for the same purposes, even if they are in the Union List, until Parliament by law says otherwise.
k: local body taxes in union list

art-279.s: "Net proceeds" of a tax means its proceeds minus the cost of collection, and the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India certifies them for any area, with that certificate being final. A law of Parliament or a Presidential order can set how proceeds assigned to States are calculated, when and how payments are made, and year-to-year adjustments.

art-279A.s: The President sets up a GST Council of the Union Finance Minister (chair), the Union Minister of State for Revenue or Finance, and a minister from each State. It recommends GST rates, exemptions, thresholds, model laws and when fuels come under GST. Decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes present and voting, the Centre's votes counting one-third and the States' two-thirds.

art-280.s: The President sets up a Finance Commission of a Chairman and four other members every five years, or earlier if needed, and Parliament sets their qualifications by law. It recommends how tax proceeds are shared between the Union and States and among States, principles for grants to States, and ways to boost State funds for Panchayats and Municipalities.

art-281.s: The President must place every Finance Commission recommendation before each House of Parliament, with a note explaining the action taken on it.

art-282.s: The Union or a State can make grants for any public purpose, even one outside the subjects on which Parliament or that State's Legislature can make laws.

art-283.s: Parliament makes laws on keeping, paying into and withdrawing from the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and public account of India, and until then the President's rules apply. Each State Legislature does the same for the State's funds, with the Governor's rules applying until then.

art-284.s: Money received by Union or State officers in their official role, other than government revenue, and money deposited with any court in India for a case, account or person, must be paid into the public account of India or of the State.

art-285.s: Union property is exempt from all State and local taxes unless Parliament by law says otherwise. Until Parliament decides, a local authority can keep taxing Union property that was taxable before the Constitution began, as long as that tax continues in the State.
k: can states tax central government property

art-286.s: No State law can tax a supply of goods or services that takes place outside the State, or during import into or export out of India. Parliament can by law set principles for deciding when a supply happens in these ways.
k: state tax on imports and exports
state cannot tax supply outside state

art-287.s: Unless Parliament by law says otherwise, a State cannot tax electricity consumed by or sold to the Government of India, or used by it or a railway company to build, maintain or run a railway. Any State tax on electricity sales must keep the price to these buyers lower, by the tax amount, than to other large consumers.

art-288.s: Unless the President orders otherwise, State laws in force before the Constitution began cannot tax water or electricity stored, generated, used, distributed or sold by an authority regulating or developing an inter-State river or river valley. A new State tax of this kind needs the President's assent, and any rate-fixing rules need the President's prior consent.
k: state tax on water and electricity

art-289.s: State property and income are exempt from Union taxes. Parliament can still allow Union taxes on a trade or business run by a State government, and its property and income, unless Parliament declares that business part of the government's ordinary functions.
k: state property exempt from union tax

art-290.s: When court or Commission costs, or pensions of people who served the Crown in India or the Union or a State, are charged on one government's Consolidated Fund but the court, Commission or service also served another government, that other government contributes. The amount is as agreed, or as set by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.
k: sharing expenses of courts and commissions

art-290A.s: Keralam pays forty-six lakh fifty thousand rupees yearly from its Consolidated Fund to the Travancore Devaswom Fund, and Tamil Nadu pays thirteen lakh fifty thousand rupees yearly to its Devaswom Fund for Hindu temples and shrines in areas transferred from Travancore-Cochin on 1 November 1956.

art-292.s: The Union government can borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, and give guarantees, within any limits Parliament sets by law.

art-293.s: A State can borrow within India on the security of its Consolidated Fund, within limits its Legislature sets by law. The Government of India can lend to States or guarantee their loans. A State still owing on a loan made or guaranteed by the Government of India needs its consent, which may carry conditions, to borrow more.

art-294.s: A transitional rule from 1950: property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations of the Dominion of India and each Governor's Province pass to the Union and the matching State, subject to adjustments for the creation of Pakistan, West Bengal, East Bengal, West Punjab and East Punjab.

art-295.s: A transitional rule from 1950: property, rights and liabilities of former Indian States matching Part B States pass to the Union where they relate to Union List matters, subject to agreements. Everything else passes to the matching Part B State's government.

art-296.s: Property that would have passed to His Majesty or a Ruler by escheat, lapse or lack of a rightful owner goes to the State where it lies, or else the Union. If a government then held it, it goes to the Union or State by its use.

art-297.s: All lands, minerals and other valuables under the ocean within India's territorial waters, continental shelf or exclusive economic zone, and all other resources of that zone, belong to the Union. Parliament sets the limits of these maritime zones by law.

art-298.s: The Union and each State can run any trade or business, acquire, hold and sell property, and make contracts. Where the Union acts outside Parliament's law-making subjects, State laws apply to it, and where a State acts outside its Legislature's subjects, Parliament's laws apply.

art-299.s: Government contracts and property transfers are made in the name of the President or the Governor and signed by persons they authorise. Neither the President, the Governor, nor the person signing is personally liable for them.

art-300.s: The Government of India can sue and be sued as the "Union of India", and a State government in the State's name, as earlier governments could. In cases pending in 1950, the Union or matching State replaces the Dominion, a Province or an Indian State.

art-300A.s: No person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law.

art-301.s: Subject to the rest of this Part, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India are free.

art-302.s: Parliament can by law restrict the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between States or within any part of India, as required in the public interest.

art-303.s: Neither Parliament nor a State Legislature can use trade and commerce powers to favour one State over another or discriminate between States. Parliament can do so only if the law declares it necessary to deal with a scarcity of goods anywhere in India.

art-304.s: A State Legislature can tax goods from other States or Union territories as it taxes similar local goods, without discrimination. It can also impose reasonable trade restrictions in the public interest, but such a Bill needs the President's prior sanction.
k: state tax on goods from other states

art-305.s: Existing laws are not affected by articles 301 and 303 unless the President orders otherwise. Nor does article 301 affect laws made before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, or stop new laws, on State monopolies covered by article 19(6)(ii).

art-307.s: Parliament can by law appoint an authority it considers suitable to carry out the purposes of articles 301 to 304 on freedom of trade, and give it powers and duties.

art-308.s: In this Part, unless the context requires otherwise, "State" does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir. That State was reorganised into Union territories in 2019, so this exclusion no longer has practical effect.
k: meaning of state in trade part

art-309.s: Parliament or a State Legislature can make laws on recruitment and service conditions for Union and State government jobs. Until it does, the President (Union posts) or Governor (State posts), or someone they direct, can make rules, and any later law overrides them.

art-310.s: Unless the Constitution says otherwise, members of defence, Union and all-India services and holders of Union posts serve at the President's pleasure, and State civil servants at the Governor's pleasure. A contract hiring a specially qualified outsider can promise compensation if the post is abolished or they must leave early without misconduct.

art-311.s: A Union or State civil servant cannot be dismissed or removed by an authority below their appointing authority, nor dismissed, removed or reduced in rank without an inquiry giving them the charges and a reasonable chance to respond. No inquiry is needed after a criminal conviction, if one is not reasonably practicable, or for State security.

art-312.s: If the Rajya Sabha resolves, by at least two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is in the national interest, Parliament can by law create all-India services common to the Union and States, including an all-India judicial service for posts of district judge and above. The Indian Administrative Service and Indian Police Service count as created this way.

art-312A.s: Parliament can by law change or cancel, even retrospectively, the pay, leave, pension and disciplinary rights of officers appointed by the Secretary of State to the Crown's civil service in India before the Constitution began who continue to serve, and the pensions of such officers who left before the 1972 amendment. Courts cannot hear disputes over their old appointment agreements.

art-313.s: A transitional rule from 1950: laws that applied to public services and posts before the Constitution began stay in force, as far as they fit the Constitution, until new provision is made.

art-315.s: There is a Public Service Commission for the Union and one for each State. Two or more States can share a Joint Commission, which Parliament can set up by law after their Legislatures pass resolutions, and the Union Commission can serve a State's needs if its Governor asks and the President approves.

art-316.s: The President appoints the Chairman and members of the Union and Joint Commissions, and the Governor appoints those of a State Commission; about half must have at least ten years of government service. Members serve six years or until age 65 (Union) or 62 (State or Joint), whichever is earlier, and cannot be re-appointed.

art-317.s: The President can remove a Commission's Chairman or member for misbehaviour only after the Supreme Court, on the President's reference, inquires and advises removal, and they can be suspended meanwhile. The President can also remove them for insolvency, outside paid work, or unfitness of mind or body, and a stake in a government contract counts as misbehaviour.

art-318.s: The President (Union or Joint Commission) or Governor (State Commission) can make regulations on the number of Commission members and staff and their service conditions. A member's conditions cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

art-319.s: After leaving office, the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission cannot take any further job under the Union or State governments. Other former Chairmen and members can only be appointed as Chairman or member of the Union Commission or as Chairman of a State Commission, within set limits, and cannot take any other government job.

art-320.s: The Union and State Public Service Commissions conduct exams for government jobs. They must be consulted, and advise, on recruitment methods, appointments, promotions, transfers, disciplinary matters, and civil servants' claims for legal costs or injury pensions, though the President or Governor can exclude some matters by regulations laid before the Legislature.

art-321.s: A law of Parliament or a State Legislature can give the Union or State Public Service Commission extra functions, covering government services and also services of local authorities, bodies set up by law, or public institutions.

art-322.s: The expenses of the Union and State Public Service Commissions, including salaries, allowances and pensions of members and staff, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or of the State.

art-323.s: Each Public Service Commission reports yearly on its work to the President (Union) or Governor (State or Joint). The report goes before Parliament or the State Legislature with a note explaining any case where the Commission's advice was not accepted.

art-323A.s: Parliament can by law set up administrative tribunals, for the Union and for States, to decide disputes about recruitment and service conditions of public employees, including those of local authorities and government-owned corporations. Such a law can set their powers and procedure and transfer pending cases to them. The text lets it shut out all courts except the Supreme Court under article 136, but the Supreme Court has ruled that High Courts' and its own writ powers cannot be removed.

art-323B.s: Parliament or a State Legislature can by law set up tribunals for disputes and offences on these subjects within its power: taxes, foreign exchange and customs, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, urban property ceilings, elections, essential goods, and rent and tenancy. The law can create tribunal levels and set procedure. The text lets it shut out all courts except the Supreme Court (article 136), but the Supreme Court has ruled that High Courts' and its own writ powers cannot be removed.

art-324.s: An Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. The President appoints the Chief Election Commissioner and other Commissioners, subject to Parliament's law; the Chief can be removed only like a Supreme Court Judge, and others only on the Chief's recommendation.

art-325.s: Each territorial constituency for Parliament or a State Legislature has one general electoral roll. No one can be kept off it, or claim a place on a special roll, only because of religion, race, caste or sex.

art-326.s: Elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are by adult suffrage: every Indian citizen aged 18 or over on the fixed date can register to vote, unless disqualified by law for non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt or illegal practice.

art-327.s: Parliament can make laws on all matters relating to elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, including preparing electoral rolls and the delimitation of constituencies.

art-328.s: A State Legislature can make laws on all matters relating to elections to its own House or Houses, including electoral rolls, but only where Parliament has not made provision.

art-329.s: Courts cannot question laws on delimitation of constituencies or allotment of seats made under articles 327 or 328. An election to Parliament or a State Legislature can be challenged only by an election petition, as provided by law.

art-330.s: Seats in the Lok Sabha are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, in each State or Union territory roughly in proportion to their share of its population; for Scheduled Tribes in Assam's autonomous districts, at least in proportion. Population means the 2001 census until figures from the first census after 2026 are published.

art-330A.s: Seats are to be reserved for women in the Lok Sabha: about one-third of all directly elected seats, including about one-third of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This takes effect only after a fresh delimitation based on the first census after the 2023 amendment came into force (article 334A).

art-331.s: If the President thought the Anglo-Indian community was not adequately represented in the Lok Sabha, the President could nominate up to two of its members. Under article 334, this power lapsed in January 2020.
k: nominated members house of the people

art-332.s: Seats in every State Legislative Assembly are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes roughly in proportion to their population share, with special rules for Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. Assam's autonomous districts get reserved seats at least in proportion to population, and only members of a Scheduled Tribe of an Assam autonomous district can contest them, though the existing mix in Bodoland constituencies is kept.

art-332A.s: Seats are to be reserved for women in every State Legislative Assembly: about one-third of all directly elected seats, including about one-third of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This takes effect only after a fresh delimitation based on the first census after the 2023 amendment came into force (article 334A).

art-333.s: If the Governor thought the Anglo-Indian community needed representation in the State Legislative Assembly and was not adequately represented, the Governor could nominate one of its members. Under article 334, this power lapsed in January 2020.

art-334.s: Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies ends 80 years after the Constitution began (January 2030). Nomination of Anglo-Indian members ended after 70 years (January 2020). Existing members continue until that House or Assembly is dissolved.
k: when does sc st reservation end

art-334A.s: Reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly starts after a delimitation based on the first census taken after the 2023 amendment came into force, and ends after 15 years, though seats continue till a date Parliament fixes by law. Seats rotate after each later delimitation as Parliament decides.

art-335.s: Claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are considered in appointments to Union and State government posts, consistent with efficient administration. This does not prevent relaxing qualifying marks, lowering evaluation standards, or reservation in promotions for them.

art-336.s: A transitional rule from 1950: for the first two years, Anglo-Indians are appointed to railway, customs, postal and telegraph posts on the same basis as before 15 August 1947, with reserved posts cut by about 10% every two years and ending after ten years. Anglo-Indians can still be appointed on merit to other posts.

art-337.s: A transitional rule from 1950: for the first three financial years, the Union and States give Anglo-Indian education the same grants as in the year ending 31 March 1948, which may then fall by 10% every three years and end after ten years. Institutions qualify only if at least 40% of yearly admissions are open to other communities.

art-338.s: The President appoints a National Commission for Scheduled Castes, with a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members, to monitor safeguards and inquire into complaints with the powers of a civil court. Its reports go to the President and before Parliament and State Legislatures, governments must consult it on major policies, and the Anglo-Indian community is also covered.

art-338A.s: The President appoints a National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, with a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members, to monitor safeguards, advise on development and inquire into complaints with the powers of a civil court. Its reports go to the President and before Parliament and State Legislatures, and governments must consult it on major policies.

art-338B.s: The President appoints a National Commission for Backward Classes, with a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members, to monitor safeguards for socially and educationally backward classes and inquire into complaints with civil court powers. Its reports go before Parliament and State Legislatures, and governments must consult it on major policies, except on States' own backward class lists.

art-339.s: The President can at any time, and had to ten years after the Constitution began, appoint a Commission to report on Scheduled Areas and the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. The Union can direct a State to draw up and carry out schemes essential for tribal welfare.
k: union directions to states for tribes

art-340.s: The President can appoint a Commission to investigate the conditions and difficulties of socially and educationally backward classes and recommend steps and grants by the Union or States to improve them. Its report, with a note on action taken, goes before both Houses of Parliament.

art-341.s: The President, after consulting the Governor in the case of a State, publicly notifies which castes, races or tribes, or groups within them, are Scheduled Castes for each State or Union territory. After that, only Parliament can change the list, by law.

art-342.s: The President, after consulting the Governor in the case of a State, publicly notifies which tribes or tribal communities, or groups within them, are Scheduled Tribes for each State or Union territory. After that, only Parliament can change the list, by law.

art-342A.s: The President, after consulting the Governor in the case of a State, notifies the Central List of socially and educationally backward classes for each State or Union territory, for Central Government purposes, and only Parliament can change it by law. Each State or Union territory can also keep its own list by law, which may differ.

art-343.s: Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union, using the international form of Indian numerals. English was to continue for official Union purposes for fifteen years, and Parliament can by law allow English or Devanagari numerals after that.
k: use of english for official purposes

art-344.s: The President had to set up a Commission five and ten years after the Constitution began to recommend wider use of Hindi, limits on English and related matters, respecting non-Hindi speakers' interests in public services. A committee of 20 Lok Sabha and 10 Rajya Sabha members reviews its advice, and the President can then issue directions.

art-345.s: A State Legislature can, by law, adopt one or more languages used in the State, or Hindi, for the State's official purposes. Until it does, English continues for the official purposes it was used for before the Constitution began.
k: can a state choose its language

art-346.s: The language currently authorised for the Union's official purposes is used for communication between States and between a State and the Union. Two or more States can agree to use Hindi between themselves.

art-347.s: If a substantial part of a State's population demands it, the President can direct that a language they speak also be officially recognised throughout the State or part of it, for purposes the President specifies.
k: recognition of minority language in state
language spoken by section of population

art-348.s: Until Parliament provides otherwise, Supreme Court and High Court proceedings and the authoritative texts of Bills, Acts, Ordinances, rules and orders are in English. A Governor, with the President's consent, can allow Hindi or a State language in High Court proceedings, except judgments, decrees and orders, and an official English translation counts for State laws made in another language.

art-349.s: A rule for the first fifteen years after the Constitution began: a Bill or amendment in Parliament on the language of courts and laws needed the President's prior sanction. The President could give it only after considering the Official Language Commission's recommendations and the parliamentary committee's report.

art-350.s: Every person can submit a request to fix a grievance to any Union or State officer or authority in any language used in the Union or in that State.
k: right to petition in any language

art-350A.s: Every State and local authority must try to provide adequate teaching in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minority groups. The President can give States directions to ensure these facilities.

art-350B.s: The President appoints a Special Officer for linguistic minorities, who investigates matters about their constitutional safeguards and reports to the President. These reports are laid before each House of Parliament and sent to the State Governments concerned.

art-351.s: The Union must promote the spread and development of Hindi so it can express all parts of India's composite culture. It should enrich Hindi with forms and expressions from Hindustani and other Eighth Schedule languages, drawing vocabulary mainly from Sanskrit and then from other languages.

art-352.s: On the Union Cabinet's written decision, the President can proclaim an Emergency in all or part of India over actual or imminent war, external aggression or armed rebellion. Both Houses must approve it within one month and every six months, by a majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting, and the Lok Sabha can end it.

art-353.s: During an Emergency, the Union can direct any State on how to use its executive power, and Parliament can make laws giving powers and duties to Union authorities even on matters outside the Union List. If the Emergency covers only part of India, these powers can extend to other States where security is threatened by activities there.

art-354.s: During an Emergency, the President can order that the rules on revenue distribution in articles 268 to 279 apply with changes, until at most the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends. Each such order is laid before each House of Parliament.

art-355.s: The Union must protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and make sure every State government is run according to the Constitution.

art-356.s: If satisfied, from the Governor's report or otherwise, that a State cannot be run according to the Constitution, the President can take over its government, except High Court powers, and give Parliament its legislative powers. Parliament must approve it within two months and every six months, up to three years; past one year needs an Emergency and Election Commission certification.

art-357.s: When Parliament holds a State Legislature's powers under article 356, it can give the President power to make the State's laws and delegate it, and the President can authorise State spending when the Lok Sabha is not sitting. Such laws stay in force after the Proclamation ends until a competent legislature changes them.

art-358.s: While an Emergency declared for war or external aggression is in operation, article 19 freedoms do not limit the State's power to make laws or take executive action, if the law states it relates to the Emergency. Such laws stop having effect, to the extent they could not otherwise be made, once the Emergency ends.

art-359.s: During an Emergency, the President can order that the right to go to court to enforce named rights in Part III, except articles 20 and 21, be suspended, along with pending cases, for the Emergency or a shorter period. Laws stating they relate to the Emergency can then override those rights until the order ends.

art-360.s: The President can proclaim a financial emergency if India's financial stability or credit is threatened, and both Houses must approve it within two months. During it, the Union can give States financial directions, including salary cuts and reserving Money Bills for the President, and the President can cut Union salaries, including those of Supreme Court and High Court judges.

art-361.s: The President and Governors do not answer to any court for acts done in office, though people can still sue the Government and a body chosen by Parliament can review the President's conduct on an impeachment charge. During their term, no criminal case or arrest order is allowed, and civil cases over personal acts need two months' written notice.

art-361A.s: No one can be sued or prosecuted for publishing a substantially true newspaper report of proceedings of Parliament or a State Legislature, unless it was done with malice. The same protection covers broadcast reports and news agency reports, but not reports of secret sittings.

art-361B.s: A party member of a legislature who is disqualified under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule cannot hold any paid political post until their term would have ended or until they are elected again, whichever comes first. A paid political post is a government office, or one in a government-owned body, unless the pay is only compensatory.

art-363.s: Except as allowed under article 143, no court, including the Supreme Court, can hear disputes arising from treaties, agreements, sanads or similar documents made before the Constitution between a Ruler of an Indian State and the Government of the Dominion of India or its predecessors.

art-363A.s: From the Twenty-sixth Amendment of 1971, no one is recognised any longer as the Ruler of an Indian State or a Ruler's successor. Privy purses are abolished, all related rights and duties end, and no one is to be paid any privy purse.

art-364.s: The President can, by public notification, direct that a law of Parliament or of a State, or an existing law, does not apply to a major port or aerodrome from a set date, or applies there only with specified exceptions or changes.

art-365.s: If a State fails to follow or carry out directions given by the Union under the Constitution, the President may treat this as a situation where the State Government cannot be carried on according to the Constitution.
k: state government cannot be carried on

art-366.s: Gives the meaning of key words used throughout the Constitution, such as agricultural income, Anglo-Indian, existing law, goods, services, goods and services tax, High Court, pension, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Union territory and tax on the sale or purchase of goods. These meanings apply unless the context requires otherwise.
k: meaning of goods and services tax

art-367.s: The General Clauses Act, 1897 guides how the Constitution is read, and laws of Parliament or a State Legislature include Ordinances of the President or a Governor. A foreign State is any State other than India, unless the President declares otherwise for certain purposes.

art-368.s: Parliament can amend the Constitution through a Bill passed in each House by a majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting, after which the President must assent. Some changes, such as to the Seventh Schedule lists or States' representation in Parliament, also need approval by at least half the State Legislatures. The clauses that barred courts from reviewing amendments were declared invalid by the Supreme Court.

art-369.s: A transitional rule from 1950: for five years, Parliament could make laws on trade, production and supply within States of goods such as cotton and woollen textiles, paper, food-stuffs, cattle fodder, coal, iron, steel and mica, as if these were in the Concurrent List. Such laws then lapsed.

art-370.s: As printed, this article gave Jammu and Kashmir temporary special arrangements, limiting which parts of the Constitution applied there. The official note records a presidential declaration that from 6 August 2019 all its clauses stopped operating except one: every provision of the Constitution applies to Jammu and Kashmir without modification.

art-371.s: The President can make the Governor of Maharashtra or Gujarat specially responsible for separate development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada and the rest of Maharashtra, or Saurashtra, Kutch and the rest of Gujarat, for fair sharing of development funds, and for fair access to technical education, vocational training and State jobs. Board reports go yearly to the Assembly.

art-371A.s: No Act of Parliament on Naga religious or social practices, customary law, justice under customary law, or land ownership and transfer applies to Nagaland unless its Assembly agrees by resolution. The Governor has special responsibility for law and order while internal disturbances continue, and runs Tuensang district, with its 35-member regional council, for ten years from the State's formation or longer if extended.

art-371B.s: The President can, by order, set up a committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly made up of members elected from the tribal areas listed in the Sixth Schedule and other members, and change the Assembly's rules so the committee works properly.

art-371C.s: The President can set up a committee of Manipur Assembly members elected from the Hill Areas and give the Governor special responsibility for it to work properly. The Governor reports to the President every year, or when asked, on how the Hill Areas are run, and the Union can give directions on them.

art-371D.s: The President can order fair opportunities in public jobs and education for people from different parts of Andhra Pradesh or Telangana, including local cadres and preference or reservation in recruitment and admissions for those who have lived or studied in the local area. The President can also set up an Administrative Tribunal for State service matters, outside the High Court's supervision.

art-371E.s: Parliament can make a law to set up a University in the State of Andhra Pradesh.

art-371F.s: Special rules for Sikkim from the Thirty-sixth Amendment of 1975: its Assembly has at least 30 members, the Assembly elected in April 1974 becomes the State Assembly with a four-year term, and Sikkim gets one seat in the Lok Sabha. The Governor has special responsibility for peace and fair advancement of all sections of the population.

art-371G.s: No Act of Parliament on Mizo religious or social practices, customary law, justice under customary law, or land ownership and transfer applies to Mizoram unless its Assembly agrees by resolution, though Central Acts already in force there before the Fifty-third Amendment of 1986 are not affected. Mizoram's Assembly has at least 40 members.

art-371H.s: The Governor of Arunachal Pradesh has special responsibility for law and order, using individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers, until the President ends it; the Governor's decision on what falls under this is final. The State's Assembly has at least 30 members.

art-371-I.s: The Legislative Assembly of Goa must have at least 30 members.

art-371J.s: The President can make the Governor of Karnataka specially responsible for a development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region, fair sharing of development funds, and fair opportunities in jobs, education and training there. This can include reserving a share of seats in the region's institutions and of State government posts there for people from the region by birth or domicile.

art-372.s: All laws in force before the Constitution began continue until a competent legislature or authority changes or repeals them, but temporary laws still expire on time. For three years after the Constitution began, the President could adapt or modify these laws to fit it, and such changes cannot be questioned in court.

art-372A.s: A transitional rule after the Seventh Amendment of 1956: the President could, by order made before 1 November 1957, adapt or modify existing laws to match the amended Constitution. These changes cannot be questioned in court, but legislatures can still amend or repeal those laws.

art-373.s: A transitional rule from 1950: until Parliament made a law under article 22(7), or for one year at most, references to Parliament and its laws in the preventive detention rules of article 22 were read as references to the President and his orders.

art-374.s: A transitional rule from 1950: Federal Court judges became Supreme Court judges, cases pending in the Federal Court moved to the Supreme Court, and earlier Federal Court judgments have the same force as Supreme Court ones. Appeals pending before the Privy Council authority in Part B States also moved to the Supreme Court.

art-375.s: All civil, criminal and revenue courts, and all judicial, executive and ministerial authorities and officers across India, continue to carry out their functions, subject to the Constitution.

art-376.s: A transitional rule from 1950: High Court judges in the Provinces became judges of the High Court of the corresponding State, with the same pay and rights, and can become Chief Justice even if not citizens of India. Judges in Part B States continue for a period the President decides, and acting or additional judges are not covered.

art-377.s: A transitional rule from 1950: the Auditor-General of India then in office became the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, with that office's salary, leave and pension rights, and continues until the end of his original term.

art-378.s: A transitional rule from 1950: members of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India became members of the Public Service Commission for the Union, and members of Provincial commissions became members of the corresponding State or Joint State commission. They continue until their original terms end.

art-378A.s: A transitional rule: the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly formed under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 lasts five years from the date set in section 29 of that Act, unless dissolved earlier, and is then dissolved automatically.

art-392.s: A transitional rule: to remove difficulties in moving from the Government of India Act, 1935 to the Constitution, the President could order temporary adaptations to the Constitution until Parliament first met, with every order laid before Parliament. Before the Constitution began, the Governor-General used these powers.
k: transition from government of india act

art-393.s: The official name of this Constitution is the Constitution of India.

art-394.s: A few articles, including this one, came into force at once. The rest of the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, the day called the commencement of the Constitution.
k: when did constitution come into force

art-394A.s: The President must publish a Hindi translation of the Constitution, signed by members of the Constituent Assembly and updated with all amendments, and a Hindi translation of every amendment. These translations carry the same meaning as the original, are revised if difficulties arise, and are the authoritative Hindi text.

art-395.s: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935, along with the laws amending or supplementing that Act, are repealed. The Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 is not repealed.

part-I.s: Names India as a Union of States and sets out its territory. Parliament can admit or set up new States, form new States and change the areas, boundaries or names of existing ones, with matching changes to the First and Fourth Schedules.

part-II.s: Sets out who became a citizen of India when the Constitution began, including people who migrated to or from Pakistan and people of Indian origin living abroad. A person who voluntarily takes foreign citizenship is not a citizen, and Parliament regulates citizenship by law.

part-III.s: Lists the Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom (including speech, and protection of life and personal liberty), the right to education, rights against exploitation, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights. It also saves certain laws and gives the right to constitutional remedies to enforce these rights.

part-IV.s: Lists the Directive Principles the State must apply in making laws, though no court can enforce them, such as a welfare-based social order, equal justice and free legal aid, village panchayats, fair work conditions and a living wage, a uniform civil code, early childhood education, protecting the environment, and separating the judiciary from the executive.

part-IVA.s: Sets out the Fundamental Duties, all in a single article (Article 51A).

part-V.s: Sets up the Union government: the President and Vice-President, the Council of Ministers and the Attorney-General; Parliament and how it passes laws and handles money; the President's power to issue Ordinances; the Supreme Court; and the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

part-VI.s: Sets up government in the States: the Governor, the Council of Ministers and the Advocate-General; the State Legislature and how it passes laws and handles money; the Governor's power to issue Ordinances; the High Courts; and subordinate courts, including district judges.

part-VII.s: This Part has been omitted. Its title covered the States in Part B of the First Schedule.

part-VIII.s: Covers how Union territories are run, including local Legislatures or Councils of Ministers for some of them, special provisions for Delhi, the administrator's power to issue Ordinances, the President's power to make regulations, and High Courts for Union territories.

part-IX.s: Covers Panchayats: the Gram Sabha, how Panchayats are formed and made up, reservation of seats, their term, disqualifications, powers, taxes and funds, a Finance Commission to review their finances, audit and elections. Courts are barred from interfering in their electoral matters. The Part also applies to Union territories, but not to certain tribal and hill areas and States, and it had a transitional rule for older Panchayat laws.

part-IXA.s: Covers Municipalities: how they and Wards Committees are formed, reservation of seats, their term, disqualifications, powers, taxes and funds, a Finance Commission, audit and elections. It also provides committees for district planning and metropolitan planning.

part-IXB.s: Covers co-operative societies: how they are incorporated, the number and term of board members, board elections, supersession of boards, audit, general body meetings, members' right to information, returns, and offences and penalties, with rules for multi-State co-operative societies and Union territories. In 2021 the Supreme Court held that this Part applies only to multi-State co-operative societies, because the amendment that added it was not ratified by half the States.

part-X.s: Covers the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas, and allows an autonomous State to be formed from certain tribal areas in Assam, with its own local Legislature or Council of Ministers or both.

part-XI.s: Divides law-making power between Parliament and the State Legislatures, including residuary powers, goods and services tax, and when Parliament can make laws on State List matters. It also covers administrative relations, inter-State river water disputes and an inter-State Council.

part-XII.s: Covers public finance: taxes only by law, the Consolidated and Contingency Funds, sharing of taxes between the Union and States, the Goods and Services Tax Council and the Finance Commission. It also covers borrowing, property, contracts and suits, and the right not to lose property except by law.

part-XIII.s: Declares freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India and sets its limits, including restrictions Parliament and the States can impose and the saving of laws for State monopolies.

part-XIV.s: Covers people serving the Union and the States: recruitment, conditions of service, tenure, rules on dismissal, removal or reduction in rank, and the All-India services. It also sets up Public Service Commissions for the Union and the States and sets out their members and functions.

part-XIVA.s: Allows administrative tribunals, and tribunals for other matters, to be set up.

part-XV.s: Places control of elections in an Election Commission and lets Parliament and State Legislatures make election laws. No one can be left off the electoral roll only because of religion, race, caste or sex, and elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies use adult suffrage. Courts cannot question delimitation laws, and an election can be challenged only by an election petition.

part-XVI.s: Reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and once delimitation is done for women, in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, and sets when reservation ends; Anglo-Indian nomination has lapsed. It sets up National Commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes, covers claims to government posts, and lets the President notify who counts as Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes.

part-XVII.s: Covers the official language of the Union and the States, the language between States and with the Union, and the language of the Supreme Court, High Courts and Acts. It also covers mother-tongue teaching at primary stage, a Special Officer for linguistic minorities and developing Hindi.

part-XVIII.s: Covers Proclamations of Emergency and their effects, the Union's duty to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance, failure of constitutional machinery in a State, suspension of Article 19 and of the right to go to court for Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21) during emergencies, and financial emergency.

part-XIX.s: Gathers miscellaneous provisions: protection of the President and Governors, protection for publishing legislative proceedings, disqualification from paid political posts, Rulers of Indian States and the end of their privy purses, major ports and aerodromes, the effect of a State not following Union directions, and definitions and interpretation.

part-XX.s: Gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and sets out the procedure for doing so.

part-XXI.s: Contains temporary, transitional and special provisions, including Article 370 on Jammu and Kashmir (which since 2019 only applies the whole Constitution there) and special provisions for Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa and Karnataka. It also covers continuing existing laws and the changeover when the Constitution began.

part-XXII.s: Gives the Constitution's short title and commencement, provides for an authoritative text in Hindi, and deals with repeals.

sch-FIRST.s: Lists the States and Union territories and the territory each covers, mostly by reference to the Acts that formed or changed them. It serves Articles 1 and 4.

sch-SECOND.s: Sets out the salaries, allowances and privileges of the President and Governors, the presiding officers of Parliament and State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Most of the rupee amounts shown have since been raised by laws made by Parliament (the President, for example, now gets five lakh rupees a month). It serves Articles 59, 65, 75, 97, 125, 148, 158, 164, 186 and 221.

sch-THIRD.s: Gives the forms of oath or affirmation for Union and State Ministers (office and secrecy), candidates for and members of Parliament and State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor-General. It serves Articles 75, 84, 99, 124, 148, 164, 173, 188 and 219.

sch-FOURTH.s: Allots the Rajya Sabha (Rajya Sabha) seats filled by representatives of each State and Union territory, 233 in total, ranging from 31 for Uttar Pradesh to 1 for several smaller States and Puducherry. Members nominated by the President come on top of these. It serves Articles 4(1) and 80(2).
k: seats per state in council of states

sch-FIFTH.s: Sets out how Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes are run in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Governor reports to the President and can direct that any Act shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or shall apply with changes. The Governor can also make regulations, for example restricting tribal land transfers or controlling money-lending, but only after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council (up to twenty members, about three-fourths of them Scheduled Tribe members of the State Assembly) and with the President's assent. The President declares Scheduled Areas, and Parliament can amend the Schedule by ordinary law. It serves Article 244(1).

sch-SIXTH.s: Provides for autonomous districts and regions in the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Each district has a District Council of up to thirty members (no more than four nominated by the Governor, the rest elected; Bodoland in Assam can have up to forty-six), and each region has a Regional Council. The Councils can make laws on local matters such as land, forests, marriage and social customs, which take effect only with the Governor's assent, and can also run village courts and levy certain taxes. It serves Articles 244(2) and 275(1).

sch-SEVENTH.s: Contains the three subject lists used under Article 246 to divide law-making power. Parliament makes laws on the Union List (such as defence, foreign affairs, citizenship, railways, banking and insurance), State Legislatures on the State List (such as police, public order, public health, agriculture and land), and both on the Concurrent List (such as criminal law, marriage, education, forests and electricity). Any subject not listed anywhere belongs to Parliament.

sch-EIGHTH.s: Lists 22 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu. It serves Articles 344(1) and 351.

sch-NINTH.s: Lists Acts and Regulations, mostly on land reform, tenancy and land ceilings, that Article 31B protects from being struck down for conflicting with Fundamental Rights. A few entries have since been removed. The Supreme Court has held that laws added on or after 24 April 1973 can still be tested against the basic structure.

sch-TENTH.s: Sets out when a member of Parliament or a State Legislature is disqualified for defection, such as voluntarily giving up party membership, voting or abstaining against the party's direction without permission (unless the party forgives it within 15 days), or an independent joining a party after election. There are exceptions for mergers agreed to by at least two-thirds of the party's legislators and for presiding officers. The Chairman or Speaker decides, and it serves Articles 102(2) and 191(2).

sch-ELEVENTH.s: Lists 29 subjects, including agriculture, minor irrigation, drinking water, rural housing, roads, education, health and sanitation, and the public distribution system, on which a State Legislature may by law give Panchayats powers and responsibilities. It serves Article 243G.

sch-TWELFTH.s: Lists 18 subjects, including urban planning, land use and building rules, water supply, sanitation and solid waste management, fire services, slum improvement and registration of births and deaths, on which a State Legislature may by law give Municipalities powers and responsibilities. It serves Article 243W.

art-243O.s: Courts cannot question laws on drawing Panchayat constituencies or allotting their seats. A Panchayat election can be challenged only through an election petition, in the way State law provides.

art-243ZO.s: The State Legislature can give every member of a co-operative society access to its books and accounts relating to their dealings, set minimum participation in meetings and services, and provide co-operative education and training for members.
